Doctor of Sciences in Public Administration · Professor

Learning that builds capability.
Research that strengthens public services.

Prof. Svitlana Chukut brings over 25 years of experience in higher education, information policy and digital governance. Her work at George Brown Polytechnic includes 17 course initiatives and more than 50 modules, using Brightspace, H5P and scenario-based assessment. She contributed to Ukraine’s national Concept for the Development of E-Governance.

Teaching and research

Professional statements

Prof. Svitlana Chukut’s approach to teaching public administration and digital governance is informed by her research on public institutions and services.

Teaching Philosophy

I want students to leave my classroom able to make and defend a public decision when the evidence is incomplete, interests conflict and the people affected have different needs.

I start with a problem a public institution could face and give students the concepts they need to work through it. In SMART CITY: FUTURE – TODAY, a simulation I designed, students apply public-management theory to a municipal decision, weigh stakeholder priorities and explain their choices. A debrief lets them revisit whose needs they considered, what evidence they used and how they would change their recommendation. I bring the same questions into discussions of digital public services and responsible AI.

In a course on digital governance, I would ask students to compare two public services, identify a barrier facing a particular group and write a brief recommending a change. I would assess the quality of the evidence, the feasibility of the proposal and how clearly students explain the trade-offs. Feedback on a draft would give them a chance to revise. In AI-related assignments, I ask students to verify claims against reliable sources, document how they used the tool and explain which judgements they made themselves.

  • Accessible by design. At George Brown Polytechnic, I developed accessible learning materials, scenario-based activities and assessments for online and blended courses in Brightspace and H5P. I design for clear navigation and manageable stages, with accessible formats and explicit criteria that help students plan their work and direct their attention to the learning task.
  • Research mentorship. I help students turn a broad interest into a question they can answer, choose a defensible method and explain the limits of their evidence. I have supervised more than 60 master’s theses and guided five doctoral researchers through successful defences. I also support students who want to develop their findings for a conference, publication or research competition.
  • Evidence for course improvement. I use student feedback and patterns in their work to decide where a case, an instruction or an assessment criterion needs revision. At Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute, student feedback placed two of my university-wide electives, Smart Cities and Fundamentals of E-Governance, in the top ten. I treat that feedback as one source of evidence alongside the work students produce.

Research Statement

How can public institutions use digital technologies to sustain essential services, earn public trust and expand participation, particularly during war and recovery?

Prof. Chukut’s research connects information policy with the design and implementation of digital public services. Her early work on cultural continuity examined how societies preserve and transmit knowledge. She applied this perspective to electronic parliaments, administrative services and government–public communication, examining how institutions make decisions visible and enable meaningful citizen participation. In 2010, she helped draft Ukraine’s national E-Governance Development Concept, bringing comparative research and institutional analysis into a national policy framework.

Prof. Chukut combines legal and policy analysis, international comparison, case studies and stakeholder consultation to trace policy from its legal basis to implementation. She has applied these methods to registered research programmes, guidance for public authorities, civil-service training and university courses. The work covers policy design, implementation and evaluation, including a social audit and work associated with the Swiss–Ukrainian EGAP programme.

  • Digital government and institutional resilience. Through Orbicom and a registered KPI project on the Sustainable Development Goals, Prof. Chukut examines how public institutions communicate and sustain services during war, and how they respond to disinformation and generative AI.
  • AI, smart cities and recovery. As principal investigator on a GISU project, Prof. Chukut leads mixed-methods research on how AI might support tourism in wartime and post-war Ukraine. The study examines economic opportunities, data governance, privacy, misinformation and cybersecurity.
  • Digital inclusion and public-sector capacity. Prof. Chukut’s publications examine access to electronic services for vulnerable groups and civil servants’ competencies in AI. Her proposals on displacement and educational reintegration investigate how people can access digital services and continue learning when ordinary provision is disrupted.

Highest scientific degree

Doctor of Sciences in Public Administration

1999 · Ukrainian Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine

Doctoral dissertation: “Reproduction of the Generational Integrity of Spiritual Culture (Managerial Aspect)”; scientific consultant: Professor Vitalii Skurativskyi.

Doctoral defence and historical record

The dissertation register records Chukut’s Doctor of Sciences defence on 29 October 1999. In Valerii Bakumenko’s chronology of Ukraine’s first Doctor of Sciences defences in Public Administration, she is the first woman listed. The three preceding defences were those of Vitalii Tron, Vasyl Shamrai and Vasyl Ryzhykh.

  • Dissertation record 0599U000486 (Ukrainian)
  • Bakumenko, V. D. (2016). First Doctors of Sciences in Public Administration in Ukraine, pp. 168–169 (Ukrainian PDF).

Timeline

Career step by step

Academic and professional appointments in Ukraine and Canada, 1993–2026.

Creative Producer, George Brown Polytechnic (Toronto)

October 2025 – April 2026

Continued developing courses and led the production of digital learning materials for multidisciplinary postsecondary projects. She designed gamified activities, simulations and branching scenarios that let learners practise decisions they would face in the workplace. She developed assessments aligned with course outcomes and current labour-market needs, selected authoritative sources for course readings and activities, and applied accessibility principles and responsible AI practices in digital production.

Content Producer, George Brown Polytechnic (Toronto)

September – October 2025

Continued course and module development for online and blended delivery. She developed gamified exercises, simulations and branching scenarios based on workplace situations, designed assessments to measure how learners applied what they had learned, and selected reliable, relevant sources to support the course content.

George Brown changed the job titles as part of a college-wide effort to cut costs and reduce staffing. Course development remained part of her work in both production roles.

Key role

Curriculum Developer, George Brown Polytechnic (Toronto)

June 2024 – September 2025

Contributed to 17 course initiatives and more than 50 practice-oriented modules across work-integrated learning, regulatory compliance, financial services, hospitality and tourism, mass timber, construction entrepreneurship, and transition to nursing practice. Designed competency-based frameworks, scenario-based activities, authentic assessments and H5P learning objects for Brightspace (D2L). Worked with academic leads, instructional designers and subject-matter experts to align materials with learning outcomes, professional standards and AODA/WCAG accessibility expectations.

Key role

Professor, Department of Theory and Practice of Management, National Technical University of Ukraine «Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute»

September 2013 – September 2025

Taught and conducted research in public administration, digital government, e-democracy, smart cities, communication, AI and sustainable development. Helped develop bachelor’s, master’s and PhD programmes and national standards for all three levels, and supported accreditation. Developed more than 10 online and hybrid courses in Moodle and supervised more than 60 doctoral and master’s research projects, advising students on research design, data collection, writing and publication. Served as PhD programme guarantor and on the master’s programme’s scientific and methodological commission (2018–2025). In 2021, she initiated and organised the Open University Student Olympiad in E-Governance and chaired its jury.

National contribution

Co-developed Ukraine’s national E-Governance Development Concept in a working group supported by the International Renaissance Foundation. The Cabinet of Ministers approved the concept by Order No. 2250-r on 13 December 2010. She also served on the Public Council of the State Committee for Informatization of Ukraine (2008–2011).

Professor and Deputy Head of the Chair of Information Policy, National Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine

October 2001 – January 2007

Developed master’s specialisations in Information Processes in Public Administration and Information Policy and Information Technologies. Designed distance-learning curricula in Information Policy and Public Relations, and designed and delivered 10 short professional training programmes for public servants. Also developed an e-governance module for master’s students through an international public administration reform project involving the Academy and the Higher School of Management and Law in Berlin.

Associate Professor, Department of Philosophy and Methodology of Public Administration, National Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine

November 1999 – September 2001

Designed and taught graduate courses in Information Society, Cultural Policy and Public Administration in the Department of Philosophy and Methodology of Public Administration. Alongside graduate teaching, delivered lectures and professional training for public servants.

Assistant Professor, Ukrainian Medical Dental Academy

August 1993 – September 1996

Taught Philosophy, Sociology, Philosophical Anthropology, Deontology in Medicine and Ethics at the Ukrainian Medical Dental Academy in Poltava. Developed curricula, syllabi, semester plans, assessment materials, reading lists and teaching resources for students at the academy.

Research agenda

Research agenda and methods

Prof. Svitlana Chukut studies how public institutions govern technology and deliver services when trust, access and continuity are under pressure. Her work brings comparative public administration and information policy together with research on digital services, civic participation and responsible AI. She has led registered research programmes, contributed to national policy, and translated findings into practitioner guides, local pilots and university teaching.

Digital government and public trust

  • E-Governance & Digital Government
  • Digital Inclusion & E-Democracy
  • Information Policy
  • Crisis & Wartime Digital Governance
  • European Integration of Digital Governance

AI, smart cities and public services

  • Smart Cities & Smart Governance
  • Artificial Intelligence in Public Administration
  • Human-Centred Digital Transformation

Information, culture and inclusion

  • Digital Culture & Cultural Diversity
  • Generational Continuity & Spiritual Culture
  • Open Data, Open Science & Open Education

Digital learning and professional capacity

  • Gamification & Microlearning
  • Generative AI in Education
  • Future-Ready Workforce & Lifelong Learning

Methods and analytical approach

  • Comparative policy analysis. Her work compares institutional arrangements and digital-government practices across jurisdictions, with attention to the conditions required for their adaptation.
  • Documentary and historical analysis. Legislation, institutional records and archives provide evidence of how public responsibilities, information policy and administrative practices have developed.
  • Case studies and programme analysis. Studies of electronic services and smart-city initiatives examine implementation in its organisational context, including participation, service continuity and access.
  • Stakeholder perspectives. Consultation and practitioner engagement inform the analysis of implementation constraints and the translation of research into guidance for public institutions.
  • Research-informed learning design. Research on digital governance, AI-assisted learning and gamification informs scenarios, teaching resources and professional-development activities.
  • Qualitative and quantitative evidence. Her portfolio includes mixed-methods projects and research on public servants’ AI competencies. The research question and available evidence determine the analytical approach.
  • Knowledge mobilisation. Publications, practitioner guides, policy contributions and teaching connect research findings with institutional decisions and professional practice.
  • Accessibility and inclusion. Her applied work considers barriers associated with disability, language and cultural context. Accessibility principles inform the design of digital learning resources.

Research projects and partnerships

The portfolio traces how questions about transparency, public participation and institutional capacity developed into research on digital services, responsible AI and recovery. Each project identifies her role, the question investigated and the outputs where documented.

Principal investigator — artificial intelligence, smart tourism and Ukraine’s recovery

2024 · GISU Research 2024

Principal investigator and research supervisor. The study uses mixed methods to assess where AI may support tourism services and economic recovery in Ukraine, and what safeguards are needed to manage privacy, data governance, misinformation and cybersecurity risks. Its policy questions concern both wartime operations and post-war recovery. The academic CV records an award of CNY 500,000.

Orbicom's Collaborative Research Projects “Digital transformation of public administration and local government: challenges and opportunities for achieving SDGs”

Mar 2023 – Sep 2025

Research collaboration through the Orbicom network and Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute. The work considers how wartime conditions reshape the way Ukrainian institutions communicate with the public and organise digital services. It also examines the implications of AI for the production and reliability of public information.

Digital transformation of public administration and local government for the Sustainable Development Goals

2023–2028

Research supervisor for KPI’s registered project No. 0123U101483. The project asks how national and local authorities can use digital transformation to advance the Sustainable Development Goals. It examines wartime public communication, disinformation and open-source intelligence, as well as how institutions respond to the risks and opportunities of generative AI.

Research contract — audit of Energoatom activities

2021

Conducted a social audit of Energoatom activities concerning employees and the public under the Environmental and Social Action Plan. The work focused on the social commitments of the Comprehensive Safety Upgrade Program for Ukrainian nuclear power units, including how the programme addressed information and consultation with affected groups. Contract No. D/0201.01/3011.01.

GISU Alliance – 2022 · Tourism / Smart Cities

Aug 2021 – Feb 2024

Research contributor through Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute. The GISU Alliance project examined business strategies for rebuilding tourism after COVID-19, including how technology could support resilience and recovery. Prof. Chukut extended the discussion to Ukraine’s wartime context through her 2023 symposium contribution on smart tourism, a topic she later pursued in a joint journal article.

The GISU Alliance presented her with a Certificate of Appreciation on 11 July 2023 for teaching in its programme on innovation, sustainability and tourism development in Ukraine.

Modern trends in the implementation of e-governance in Ukraine: best practices

2018–2021 in the departmental register

Research supervisor, state registration No. 0118U100305. Impact of e-governance on social transformations

Research supervisor, state registration No. 0115U000019. The team examined e-parliament, civic participation in smart cities and local e-governance. Theoretical, methodological, organizational and institutional principles of e-governance implementation

Jan 2010 – Dec 2011

Research supervisor, state registration No. 0201U004833. Led the Academy team in comparing models for organising e-governance at national, regional and local levels, with Olha Zahvoiska responsible for project execution. The work fed directly into policy drafting and a master’s course in e-governance.

Final report and documented outputs

Final report of the Academy research project carried out by the Information Policy Chair under Prof. Svitlana Chukut's scientific supervision (responsible executor: Olha Zahvoiska), completed in December 2011 (180 pp., 152 sources). The project studied the patterns of e-governance formation in Ukraine and abroad, its essence, methods and principles and its institutional implementation models at the national, regional and local levels, and the foreign experience of master's programmes in e-governance. Its team took a direct part in drafting the Electronic Government Development Concept for Ukraine and its implementation plan, and in drafting the statutes of the profile central executive bodies. The project's outputs include the methodical and information-analytical materials of the normative course of the same name for the master's specialty "E-Governance", the first two issues of the international journal "E-Governance", and conference and E-Governance Days materials; its results were implemented in the profile unit of the Secretariat of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine and the State Agency for Science, Education and Informatisation of Ukraine, and used in the Academy's teaching.

Research supervisor, with Olha Zahvoiska responsible for project execution (No. 0109U003027). The team developed teaching guidance and a textbook on communication in public administration. It piloted civic-responsibility work in Kherson oblast and Crimea, and its results were used by the Public Relations Department of the Cabinet Secretariat.

Selected research proposals

  • Digital Inclusion of Vulnerable Groups in Smart Cities (2022) — Proposal to the National Research Foundation of Ukraine. Proposed measuring digital inclusion, assessing needs through mixed methods, comparing policy scenarios and developing a roadmap for more equitable access to smart-city services.
  • Digital Skills / Ukrainian Forced Female Migrants in Latvia (2022) — Ukrainian–Latvian proposal examining how access to technology and digital skills could support the social inclusion of Ukrainian women forcibly displaced to Latvia.
  • Digital & Educational Reintegration of Youth from De-Occupied Territories (2022) — Proposal on how digital tools and educational provision could help young people from liberated and temporarily occupied territories reconnect with Ukrainian education, framed in the context of national security.
  • Digital Educational Reintegration of Youth (SDGs) (2021) — Proposal linking digital access and educational continuity for young people from temporarily occupied territories with Ukraine’s Sustainable Development Goals.

Defended doctoral dissertations

Guarantor of KPI’s PhD programme in Public Governance and Administration (2018–2025) and member of specialised dissertation defence councils.

  • 2025Anna Ishchenko

    Digital Transformation of Public Administration in the Context of Gender Mainstreaming

    PhD in Public Governance and Administration

    The dissertation examines how gender mainstreaming can improve access to digital public services and shape the transformation of Ukraine’s civil service. It combines a survey of public officials, in-depth interviews with experts, and analysis of legislation and policy documents. It traces the development of digital accessibility in Ukraine and uses the empirical findings on digital competencies to formulate recommendations for gender-responsive policy and professional development in the civil service.

    View dissertation record →
  • 2018Valeriy Dmytrenko

    Mechanisms for Implementing E-Governance at the Local Level

    Candidate of Sciences in Public Administration

    The dissertation develops a framework for implementing e-governance at the local level. It reviews Ukraine’s legal arrangements and compares international practices, including German coordination across levels of government and European interoperability principles. Its recommendations connect technical standards with municipal governance, including coordination among national, regional and local authorities, citizen involvement in decision-making, and urban living labs for testing services with the people who use them.

    View dissertation record →
  • 2009Tetiana Ilyuk

    Government Information Campaigns on European Integration in Poland: A Theoretical and Methodological Approach

    Candidate of Sciences in Public Administration

    The dissertation compares Poland’s government communication on European integration in 1999–2004 with Ukraine’s in 2004–2007. It examines campaign design through target audiences, messages, channels and feedback, and links the effectiveness of Poland’s campaign to the sequencing and execution of its main stages. It refines the classification of campaigns by purpose and offers recommendations for informing the Ukrainian public about European integration.

    View dissertation record →Read the dissertation synopsis (PDF) →
  • 2009Oleksandr Poprotskyi

    Formation of Public Opinion: Mechanisms of State Regulation of Information Flows

    Candidate of Sciences in Public Administration

    The dissertation studies the formation and expression of public opinion under the influence of information flows. It proposes a theoretical model of how shared attitudes form and analyses the channels through which they are expressed, including surveys, petitions, public debate and the media. It examines how public authorities can support open expression and how regulation can address covert influence while preserving the conditions for public opinion to develop freely.

    View dissertation record →
  • 2003Oleg Grygor

    Formation of the Information Society in Ukraine in the Context of Integration into the European Union (Public-Administration Aspect)

    Candidate of Sciences in Public Administration

    The dissertation examines the policy and institutional conditions for developing Ukraine’s information society as the country pursues European integration. It reviews European approaches to coordination and legislation and considers Ukraine’s needs in telecommunications, public-sector information systems and personal data protection. Its recommendations include a state programme to encourage the use of information and communication technologies and an information and analysis centre to support national and local authorities.

    View the original presentation (Ukrainian PDF)
    Presentation overview

    The presentation traces Ukraine’s early digital-government reforms, including electronic trust services and the adoption of a digital economy strategy. It uses public-service examples to show how those reforms affected practical delivery.

    The comparison centres on Estonia’s electronic identity card and X-Road data exchange. The Ukrainian case follows the adaptation of X-Road as Trembita and a 2017 electronic service for registering land-lease agreements.

    Prylepko recommends informing the public, securing funding, and training or retraining public officials. The presentation also cites a conference paper from November 2017 and reports that Rent-Alliance used the research results.

Trust

Expert roles

The expert and trust roles: research evaluation, doctoral programmes, education quality and government working groups.

2010–2011

Policy and regulatory development for digital government

While heading the Department of Information Policy at the National Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine, Prof. Svitlana Chukut contributed to policy proposals on e-governance and the information society. The department’s 2010–2011 work addressed executive coordination, draft regulatory instruments, public services and training for civil servants.

The Cabinet of Ministers approved Ukraine’s E-Governance Development Concept, which she co-developed, on 13 December 2010 and approved its implementation plan on 26 September 2011. The Academy documents below present proposals prepared during that period.

Prof. Chukut’s 2007–2011 departmental report records her participation in developing and discussing the draft Law on Access to Public Information. It also documents collaboration with the Cabinet Secretariat, the Council of Ministers of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, and the Kherson regional and Novovorontsovka district administrations on research and its practical application.

The 2009 forum recommendations also called for a national concept, common standards and dedicated civil-service training. Academy correspondence shows how the National Academy sought support for professional recognition of e-governance and how the programme’s design responded to the staffing needs of state authorities.

People & shared work

Professional collaboration

Partnerships with public authorities, universities, technology specialists and international research networks connect Prof. Svitlana Chukut’s work on digital government with public policy, professional training and joint publications.

National government and public policy

Co-developed Ukraine’s national E-Governance Development Concept. The Cabinet Secretariat and other public authorities applied research on digital government and government–public communication. Her work also included the State Committee for Informatization, the Presidential Secretariat’s working group on information systems for local administrations, and the National Security and Defence Council’s interagency working group.

In 2011, she was appointed to a State Committee for Television and Radio Broadcasting commission that brought together representatives of public institutions, educational bodies, media law, publishing and professional organisations. Commission mandate and appointment details

The 2010 proposals identified the Cabinet Secretariat’s information resources and technology unit, the Presidential Administration, ministries, the State Committee for Informatization and the State Service of Special Communications among the bodies that would coordinate or carry out the proposed measures. In 2011, the department also outlined possible cooperation with the European Union on civil-service training, policy design and pilot projects.

Explore her policy and regulatory workScholarly and government service

Regional authorities and municipal government

Worked with the Kherson Regional State Administration on public communication, applied research and the regional Presidential Personnel Reserve project. Research recommendations were used by its press and information department and by the Novovorontsov district education department, where she supported the pilot School of E-Governance. Served on Brovary’s e-governance working group (2006–2009) and joined the Scientific and Technical Council of the Kyiv Regional State Administration in 2021 to assess local development projects. Contributed to a civic-responsibility project with the Council of Ministers of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.

International partnerships and training

Served as an expert on the Swiss-supported E-Governance for Accountability and Community Participation (EGAP) programme (2015–2017). Earlier, worked on a German-supported civil-service training project with the Higher School of Management and Law in Berlin, developing an e-governance module for master’s students (2005–2008). Collaborated with Estonian experts on Ukraine’s national concept, and later with researchers through GISU and Orbicom on smart tourism, digital governance and the Sustainable Development Goals.

Research projects and partners

Ukrainian universities and national higher education standards

As chair of the Ministry of Education and Science’s Subcommission 281 (2016–2019), Prof. Svitlana Chukut worked with colleagues from Ukrainian universities to discuss, develop and refine the national higher education standards for Public Governance and Administration. This work brought together academic perspectives on graduate competencies and learning outcomes, and on how programmes could prepare students for work in public authorities and local government.

National bachelor’s standard for specialty 281

Cross-department collaboration at Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute

At KPI, Prof. Chukut collaborated across departments, including with colleagues in information technology. She brought a public administration perspective to questions that require both policy and technical expertise, such as how public services are designed, how institutions exchange information, and what digital competencies students and public servants need.

Joint research and publications

Joint publications range from comparative studies of interoperability and public service delivery to research on how institutions adapt during crises. With Anna Ischenko, Prof. Chukut studied Ukrainian public servants’ skills in using AI tools. With Alla Karapoziuk, she examined the digitisation of archival processes. Her team’s study of smart tourism brought together research on wartime adaptation, technology and economic recovery, while work with Olha Zahvoiska and Yana Tsymbalenko produced a university textbook on e-governance.

Books

Books and contributions

Monographs, textbooks, edited collections and chapters by Prof. Svitlana Chukut as author, co-author or editor. Entries identify her role and link to the text or bibliographic record where available.

2022 · 268 pp.

Fundamentals of Electronic Governance

Prof. Svitlana Chukut, Olha Zahvoiska and Yana Tsymbalenko. An electronic textbook published by National Technical University of Ukraine «Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute».

An eight-chapter introduction combining concepts, international comparisons, Ukrainian experience and research-based learning activities.

Description

This 268-page electronic textbook, published by Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute in 2022, provides a structured introduction to e-governance for undergraduate students in Specialty 281, Public Administration and Management, including the Administrative Management and E-Governance programmes. It also supports the university-wide course Fundamentals of Electronic Governance. Prof. Svitlana Chukut is a co-author and the responsible editor, alongside co-authors Olha Zahvoiska and Yana Tsymbalenko.

Its eight chapters connect conceptual foundations with the institutional and societal dimensions of digital government. They examine models of e-governance and implementation barriers; United Nations assessment methods and indices, including e-government development, online services, telecommunications infrastructure, human capital, e-participation and local online services; and the development of e-governance in Ukraine.

The treatment of digital public services addresses service maturity, interoperability, inclusion of vulnerable groups and the Diia portal, with examples from Austria and Denmark. Further chapters examine e-democracy, electronic petitions, e-parliament and electronic voting, including Council of Europe standards and experience from the United States and Estonia. The final chapter considers network warfare and the COVID-19 pandemic as challenges for digital governance and democratic participation.

The teaching framework extends beyond subject knowledge. The introduction identifies skills in evidence gathering, analysis, recommendations, teamwork and decision-making. The textbook includes individual research assignments, team-project requirements and suggested topics, a glossary and references. These elements support independent inquiry and discussion of how institutions can introduce digital services while considering participation, inclusion and implementation risks.

Domestic and Foreign Experience of Implementing E-Governance

Proceedings of the first E-Governance Day (Kyiv, 14 May 2008), National Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine. General editor: Prof. Svitlana Chukut; co-editor: Olha Zahvoiska.

Description

Proceedings of the scientific-practical conference held at the National Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine for E-Governance Day on 14 May 2008 (Kyiv, 2008, 128 pp.; general editors Prof. Svitlana Chukut and Olha Zahvoiska; recommended by the Academy's Academic Council, protocol No. 148/8-4 of 28 August 2008). The volume presents scientific-practical approaches, research results and implementation experience in e-governance and e-democracy: its sections cover e-governance at the central level and at the local level, electronic services, e-democracy, and the main tasks of e-government — including the role of the Microsoft corporation in carrying them out — and it closes with the recommendations adopted from E-Governance Day 2008. The materials, drawn from the leading domestic and foreign experience of e-governance in central, local and regional administration, are addressed to public-administration and business practitioners, heads of state and local authorities, enterprises, institutions and civil-society organisations, and to everyone who studies, researches, implements or uses e-governance technologies.

2006 · 663 pp.

Information Policy — a textbook

Heorhii Pocheptsov and Prof. Svitlana Chukut · Kyiv, Znannia

Description

A fundamental study guide offering a comprehensive examination of the theoretical, legal and managerial foundations of information policy in the context of building the information society, integrating the approaches of public administration, political science, law and the theory of strategic communications. Prof. Svitlana Chukut's authorial contribution covers the institutional-managerial and digital blocks of the discipline: the theoretical and methodological foundations of implementing electronic government, the stages of the digital transformation of public administration and the models of electronic democracy; a comparative analysis of successful world practices of information-society and e-governance development (the European Union, the USA, Great Britain, Estonia, Singapore); and the mechanisms of Ukraine's state information policy, the protection of information resources, citizens' access to public information and overcoming the digital divide. One of the first basic academic editions in Ukraine to integrate e-governance into a general course on state information policy, the book contains a complete teaching and methodological complex — a glossary, review questions, topics for research papers and the normative base — and is widely used in training specialists in public administration, political science, international relations and information security.

2007

Information Policy in Ukraine — lecture outline

Prof. Svitlana Chukut, Tetiana Dzhyha. Lecture outline, National Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine, Kyiv, 2007.

Description

Lecture outline for the course "Information Policy in Ukraine" by Prof. Svitlana Chukut and Tetiana Dzhyha (Kyiv, 2007, 94 pp.). The outline sets out the main theoretical and methodological foundations of the discipline: it describes the key provisions of information policy, discloses the activity of the central authorities in the field of information, presents the main principles of foreign countries' information policy on building the information society, analyses the legal regulation of the information sphere and the main aspects of implementing e-governance in Ukraine and worldwide, and focuses on the principal problem and key issues of communicative policy in government bodies. Its chapters cover Ukraine's state information policy and the central authorities in the information sphere, foreign information policy on building the information society, and the legal regulation of the information sphere. The guide is intended for master's students of the National Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine in the "Public Administration" specialty, and is also useful for practitioner managers, information-policy specialists, students and lecturers of economic specialties.

1999

The Genesis of Spiritual Culture (the Management Dimension)

Author · Monograph. Kyiv: Ukrainian Academy of Public Administration. — 256 pp.

Description

Prof. Chukut's monograph (Ukrainian Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine, Kyiv, 1999; approved for publication by the Academy's Academic Council on 24 December 1998) studies the genesis of spiritual culture through the lens of public administration. Written at the turn of the millennium, it opens from the era's spiritual-culture problems — the devaluation of universal values, "creativity to order" measured by money and media accompaniment, the dominance of mass culture, the loss of trust in society's ideals, and the tension between uncritical borrowing of foreign culture and one-sided use of the national heritage. The first chapter traces the mutual conditioning of spiritual culture and state administration from the Ancient world through Hobbes ("the state as a precondition of culture") and Locke ("tradition and civil society"), German classical philosophy and the dialectical-materialist conception of history to the management of cultural continuity in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The second develops a methodology of continuity (succession): spiritual culture as a phenomenon of social life, its continuity characteristics and research methods, its subjects — the ruling elite as the subject of formal continuity and the creative elite of informal continuity — and its mechanisms, in which the ideal is the goal, choice the driver, and public opinion and values the medium. The third examines the forms of continuity — tradition as the principal form, the stereotype as its rudiment, innovation, ritual, habitus, archetype and symbol, and language as the transitional link between forms and means, including the language of politicians and its functioning in contemporary Ukrainian society. The fourth turns to the means: cultural heritage, social institutions and technical means, above all mass media and the computer production of information, within a national system of mass communication. An afterword draws the conclusions into state cultural policy — the support and management of culture.

Description

A chapter written with Olha Zahvoiska for the collective monograph "European Benchmarks of Public Administration" (Kyiv, 2023), in its section on European identity and cultural diversity. It examines what cultural diversity means inside a smart city — inclusive digital infrastructure, multilingual interfaces, digitally preserved heritage, cultural events and data-informed cultural planning — and sets out the European Union's approaches and legal framework for protecting it. 6 citationsProf. Svitlana Chukut’s Google Scholar profile

2008

E-Democracy: Definition and Main Stages

Author · In Domestic and Foreign Experience of Implementing E-Governance

Description

Prof. Chukut's paper in the E-Governance Day 2008 proceedings (pp. 89–95). She defines e-democracy as the state ensuring the necessary preconditions for citizens to participate in developing and adopting state decisions with the help of modern information and communication technologies, and explains that e-governance builds the trust between government and citizens on which it rests — through participation in decision-making, openness, accountability and the prevention of corruption. She sets out the main stages of e-democracy's formation: e-informing, a one-way flow from state bodies to citizens (access to documents, catalogues, registers and indexes, published draft laws and white and green papers, online reports and guides, via email, web portals, mobile communication, information kiosks and discs — with the attendant problems of confidential information, state secrets, privacy and national security); e-consultation, in which the government asks citizens' opinion online and receives requests, complaints, proposals and survey answers in a limited two-way relationship hindered by the digital divide; e-participation, citizens' active, feedback-based involvement in decision-making and policy-making through government and public forums and chats, interactive games and virtual workspaces; and e-partnership, in which responsibility for decisions is shared by both sides on a basis of mutual trust — a stage still in its infancy. She closes with the problems to be solved — digital inequality, access for people with disabilities, ICT illiteracy, staffing, technical capacity, financing, legal status and accountability, security and privacy — and the ways to solve them, from ensuring access and re-engineering the civil service to amending legislation and combining ICT with traditional means.

1999

Spiritual culture in Ukraine's humanitarian policy

Author · Chapter. 'Programme Ukraine 2010'. Kyiv: Ukrainian Academy of Public Administration

Description

A scientific and methodological development prepared at the Ukrainian Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine (Kyiv, 1999), setting out how spiritual culture figures in Ukraine's humanitarian policy. Its first part places culture within state-building: culture as a society's unwritten beliefs, evaluations and accepted rules — analysed through technology, economy, social organisation, religion and symbolism — and spiritual culture not as a frozen result but as the process of creating, accumulating, transmitting and using cultural acquisitions, whose core mechanism is continuity, the reproduction of a generation's cultural integrity. The second part examines Ukraine's state cultural policy: against the command-administrative concept of "managing culture", which subordinated culture to politics and economics, it sets the concept of "supporting culture" recognised by developed democracies and grounded in culture's intrinsic value, while arguing that the cultural sphere reaches far beyond the arts — to education, science, freedom of conscience and of speech — as in UNESCO's definition of cultural policy as the sum of a society's conscious actions aimed at cultural goals. The third part works through nine directions of state policy in spiritual culture: legislative support, the information sphere, cultural heritage, language policy, rituals, ceremonies and holidays, the development of the cultural and artistic sphere, the cultures of national minorities, youth culture, and international cooperation — with the Ministry of Culture and Arts as the central executive body implementing policy in the field.

1 citationProf. Svitlana Chukut’s Google Scholar profile
Artificial intelligence in public administration: challenges and threats

Conference theses in the proceedings of the XII International Conference "Contemporary Problems of Management" (Kyiv, 24 November 2023, pp. 147–150). Prof. Chukut notes that the risks of ICT in public administration have grown sharply with artificial intelligence — a field opened for government by the OECD's "Hello World" report — and, since Ukraine's EU membership bid makes European practice directly relevant, examines the European Union's approach: investment through Digital Europe and Horizon Europe, the European strategy for data, and the risk-based legal framework agreed in December 2023. She explains the AI Act's tiers: unacceptable-risk systems are banned (cognitive behavioural manipulation, social scoring, biometric categorisation, real-time remote biometric identification, with narrow law-enforcement exceptions); high-risk systems — most of them in public administration, from critical infrastructure and education to employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration and legal interpretation, including systems influencing elections — require assessment before deployment and throughout their life cycle, with citizens gaining rights to complain and to explanations; generative AI must disclose AI-generated content, prevent illegal content and publish summaries of training data, with systemic-risk general-purpose models evaluated and incidents reported; limited-risk systems owe minimal transparency, such as labelling deepfakes. Non-compliance fines run from 7.5 million euros or 1.5 percent of turnover to 35 million euros or 7 percent. She also points to the ELISE platform's open dataset of public-sector AI cases (143 by December 2023) and to CitizenLab's use of natural-language processing for civic participation.

Orbicom 'Digital transformation of public administration for SDGs'

How can governments and cities go digital in a way that also helps meet the Sustainable Development Goals — the UN's global goals for health, education, equality and the environment? This international Orbicom network project (March 2023 – September 2025) studies that question, and Prof. Svitlana Chukut takes part as a researcher associated with Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute, where she leads the university's registered initiative research theme 'Digital transformation of state administration and local self-government: challenges and opportunities for achieving the SDGs' (state registration No. 0123U101483) — fundamental research intended to produce methodological documents and analytical materials. The work runs in three strands: digitalisation of public administration at state and local levels, including her papers on organising electronic services in wartime (with Ye. Karpenko) and on digitalising archives (with A. Karapoziuk); smart cities and artificial intelligence, including the smart-tourism study, smart energy systems using big data (with L. Shumska) and the challenges and threats of artificial intelligence in public administration; and the impact of digitalisation on social processes and public administration. In the first reporting period alone (March 2023 – May 2024), the theme produced 12 articles in professional (category B) journals; student research was prepared for international competitions — a work by O. Shyts and L. Shumska took 1st place at the international competition on management, social and behavioural sciences in implementing sustainable development — and for the national Civil Service Day youth competition; and two project proposals were drafted: a Ukrainian–Latvian project on digital skills and access to digital technologies for Ukrainian forced migrant women in Latvia, and a proposal to the National Research Foundation of Ukraine on the digital and educational reintegration of young people from de-occupied and temporarily occupied territories. The results go straight into teaching: they were implemented in her courses — Fundamentals of E-Governance, Smart Cities, E-Democracy, E-Governance and E-Democracy, and Strategic Directions of E-Governance Development — five distance courses were developed and certified on the Sikorsky (Moodle) platform, and the team presented at four international conferences and seminars, including the 2023 GISU research symposium.

Fundamentals of Electronic Governance: a textbook Source

This 268-page electronic textbook, published by Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute in 2022, provides a structured introduction to e-governance for undergraduate students in Specialty 281, Public Administration and Management, including the Administrative Management and E-Governance programmes. It also supports the university-wide course Fundamentals of Electronic Governance. Prof. Svitlana Chukut is a co-author and the responsible editor, alongside co-authors Olha Zahvoiska and Yana Tsymbalenko.

Its eight chapters connect conceptual foundations with the institutional and societal dimensions of digital government. They examine models of e-governance and implementation barriers; United Nations assessment methods and indices, including e-government development, online services, telecommunications infrastructure, human capital, e-participation and local online services; and the development of e-governance in Ukraine.

The treatment of digital public services addresses service maturity, interoperability, inclusion of vulnerable groups and the Diia portal, with examples from Austria and Denmark. Further chapters examine e-democracy, electronic petitions, e-parliament and electronic voting, including Council of Europe standards and experience from the United States and Estonia. The final chapter considers network warfare and the COVID-19 pandemic as challenges for digital governance and democratic participation.

The teaching framework extends beyond subject knowledge. The introduction identifies skills in evidence gathering, analysis, recommendations, teamwork and decision-making. The textbook includes individual research assignments, team-project requirements and suggested topics, a glossary and references. These elements support independent inquiry and discussion of how institutions can introduce digital services while considering participation, inclusion and implementation risks.

Ensuring social inclusion in smart cities: challenges and current trends Source

The study unpacks the concepts of digital inequality, the digital divide, digital illiteracy and digital and social inclusion, showing how digital inequality deepens social inequality. It reviews the legal frameworks at international and EU level and the practice of individual smart cities such as Vienna, and derives the core requirements for accessibility when modern technologies are not adapted to the most vulnerable citizens. Ukrainian experience is then assessed against those requirements, and ways of securing inclusion in Ukraine are proposed.

Communication strategies in public management and administration: foreign and Ukrainian experience Source

After defining communication, communication strategies and communicative policy, the article compares how such strategies are built and implemented in Europe, North America and Asia — Madrid's Consul participation project, Canada's citizen-focused strategy and Bangladesh's local-level model. It argues that a strategy works only when the roles of each side are clearly defined, turning an organisation's core idea into key messages for each audience. Ukrainian practice is analysed at state and local level, through the Verkhovna Rada and the Merefa city council.

Interpreting 'sustainable development' in Ukraine's public administration Source

The work gathers the arguments and counter-arguments in the scholarly debate over how 'sustainable development' is understood in Ukrainian political documents — a meaning shaped by political usage and by translation from English rather than by research findings alone. Comparing voluntary national reviews of the countries whose experience Ukraine draws on (2017–2020) with Ukrainian scholarship and practice, it shows how divergent readings affect public engagement, partnership-building and e-governance. It concludes that Ukrainian public administration must re-evaluate its applied approaches, since the concept's ambiguity leaves the country without a clear strategy or stable goals.

The organisational and legal context of Ukraine's government action on sustainable development Source

Ukraine, the article notes, imports foreign sustainable-development experience and adapts it, rather than exporting its own — and its scholarship likewise adapts foreign concepts. The authors compare how Ukraine and the countries it learns from have built organisational and advisory structures responsible for sustainable development. They find a gap between the concept's legal and scholarly definitions in Ukraine, which keeps those structures being created and abolished in turn and destabilises policy direction.

Public management and COVID-19: challenges and digital transformation Source

COVID-19 acted as a catalyst that forced change in public management at an accelerated pace, as governments had to decide quickly under force-majeure pressure. Beyond the challenges already set by the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the pandemic deepened the digital divide, poverty and hunger and posed a real threat to citizens' lives. The paper frames these compounded pressures as the starting point for the digital transformation of public management.

Public management and COVID-19: challenges and digital transformation Source

Conference theses in which Prof. Chukut treats the COVID-19 pandemic as a catalyst of accelerated change in public administration. Following the World Bank, she groups the challenges into health, the economy and taxes, adds the corruption risks of emergency procurement, and notes how the crisis exposed weak coordination, fragile institutions, poor accountability and patronage — together with the danger that governments use the emergency to usurp power and restrict rights. She sets out the OECD's directions for government action in a pandemic, from public trust and digital government to risk management and public integrity, and the role of digital transformation: as the UN's Liu Zhenmin observed, digital technologies let governments keep communicating and delivering services online throughout the pandemic, even as privacy and disinformation problems sharpened. The theses present the UN Compendium of digital government initiatives responding to COVID-19 and examine France's state-built tools in detail — above all Tchap, the secure government messenger run by the Interministerial Digital Directorate (over 200,000 users by November 2021), alongside state web- and audio-conferencing, the Osmose professional-communities platform and the Resana collaborative workspace. She concludes that responses should adapt government operating, service and citizen-interaction models to digital tools, build collective action on trust — "come together while staying apart" — and develop effective, inclusive and accountable government.

APA 7Chukut, S. A. (2021). Public management and COVID-19: Challenges and digital transformation [Plenary presentation]. 11th Contemporary Problems of Management International Conference, Kyiv, Ukraine. https://ktpu.kpi.ua/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/spu2021.pdf

Audit of management and stakeholder engagement systems, Energoatom

Making a nuclear power plant safer is not only about equipment: the upgrades affect the people who work at the plants and the communities who live around them, and those people need to be properly informed and involved. In 2021 Prof. Svitlana Chukut carried out, as a project executor, an audit of the social side of that work at SE NNEGC 'Energoatom', Ukraine's nuclear energy operator. The audit covered the company's activity on social issues — concerning its personnel and the population — during implementation of the Complex (Consolidated) Programme for improving the safety of Ukraine's nuclear power plant units and the Plan of environmental and social measures, under a research contract between Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute and Energoatom (No. D/0201.01/3011.01); the customer side was led by the research-topic head, Anatolii Melnychenko. From 27 August to 20 September 2021, the work combined the audit itself with methodological, analytical and organisational support of the sociological research. Its core was a review and analysis of whether Energoatom's management system and its system of informing and engaging stakeholders comply with Ukrainian legislation, the requirements of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and best world practice. The work also included expert analysis of the company's documentation, collection of additional data and, where needed, checks directly at nuclear power plant sites, followed by a final analysis and discussion of the results with the customer. The result was a scientific (audit) report with an executive summary in Ukrainian, Russian and English, and the signed acceptance act confirms that the works were completed in full.

APA 7Audit of management and stakeholder engagement systems, Energoatom [Research project]. (2021). Energoatom.

Projects · 2021 · Project executor
GISU 'Smart Cities & Tourism Research Projects'

How can Ukraine's tourism keep working during a war — and rebuild afterwards? That is the question behind this GISU Alliance research on smart cities and tourism, in which Prof. Svitlana Chukut takes part for Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute. Drawing on in-depth interviews with experts, the work looks at how tourism businesses coped with the combined shocks of the pandemic and the full-scale war — money problems, closures and staff leaving — and sets out the approaches that helped: going digital, offering services remotely, tailoring offers to each traveller, and new forms such as military, solidarity and virtual tourism. The point is practical: with a lighter tax burden, clearer rules and stronger professional expertise, Ukraine's tourism can recover and come back more resilient.

APA 7GISU 'Smart cities & tourism research projects' [Research project]. (2021–). GISU Alliance.

The formation of Ukrainian scholarly thought on the history of domestic e-governance Source

Based on a decade of scholarship across public administration, political science, economics, law, history and technical sciences, the authors characterise the current state of Ukrainian thought on the history of domestic e-governance. They map the main research directions and theoretical frameworks, and outline the gaps and controversies that still need study. The discourse is divided into six stages, from the 1990s awareness of new technologies to a sixth stage, begun in 2019, of intensive development, new theoretical models and a consolidated research base.

Best European and Ukrainian e-service practices for vulnerable populations Source

The article surveys EU practice in supporting people with disabilities and pensioners through electronic services — including annual monitoring of digital public services — and the projects that encourage people with limitations to use modern ICT, with Denmark's directions highlighted. Ukrainian provision is then analysed for quality and accessibility, and found legally wanting: the law sets almost no requirement to adapt e-services to vulnerable groups or to prioritise them. The authors develop the Accessibility Index of Electronic Services Use in Ukraine (AIES) to measure take-up, accessibility and quality.

Blockchain or e-document management: implementation trends in Ukraine's executive bodies Source

The article examines how electronic document circulation is being implemented in Ukraine's executive authorities, with special attention to blockchain — the modern technology of distributed registers. Written with Valerii Dmytrenko, the article treats interoperability as the precondition without which electronic government cannot work, at either the local or the national level. From the Internet of Things to Smart City: problems and prospects Source

Conference paper in the proceedings "Internet of Things: Problems of Legal Regulation and Implementation" (scientific-practical conference, Kyiv, 24 October 2017, pp. 83–85). Against the background of continuing urbanisation — over 2.5 billion more city dwellers in the coming decades — and the spread of information and communication technologies and the Internet of Things, which improve quality of life while sharpening the problems of personal-data security, privacy and digital inequality, the paper examines current trends in smart-city development through the "Smart Dubai" strategy. Dubai's experience — over 100 smart initiatives and over 1,000 smart services launched by some twenty government departments and private-sector partners in under three years, and the Smart Dubai 2021 roadmap, which sets human happiness as the key indicator of success and pursues an efficient, seamless, safe and personalised city across six strategic dimensions: smart living, smart economy, smart governance, smart mobility, smart environment and smart people — is assessed as a model of the city-innovation approach based on cooperation between administrations, companies, the research community and citizens. The paper concludes that this experience can serve Ukraine, provided citizens and their needs — not developer companies — guide smart-city strategies, with account taken of each city's specific problems and advantages.

Drawing on the United Nations e-government surveys from 2003 to 2014, the article tracks how the Emirates' online services matured — including the sharp 2010 fall in its index, which it attributes to a change in the UN's calculation methodology rather than to a real decline. Smart city or e-city: modern approaches to understanding the implementation Source

The article sets the two terms side by side and asks what each one actually means for local government. It distinguishes two readings of the "smart city": a corporate one, promoted by large IT companies to sell products and automate every urban process, and a sustainable-development one, in which technology serves residents' quality of life across all spheres of city life. Against the first it weighs the risks — loss of privacy, total control over citizens and the devaluation of public participation in decisions — and illustrates both readings with foreign and Ukrainian practice. It closes with the main problems holding back local e-governance in Ukraine and the possibilities for overcoming them.

The state of public administration of the information sphere in Ukraine Source

The chapter surveys how Ukraine's information sphere was governed at the turn of the 2000s and where that governance was failing. It documents the pressure on independent media — censorship attempts, selective state support and punitive damages claims — that drew concern from the Council of Europe, and backs the picture with the period's statistics: more than 10,000 registered periodicals, of which only about 6,500 actually appeared; book output down to 0.3 copies per capita; and 791 television and radio organisations operating on 931 licences, most of them loss-making. It concludes that a stable national television and radio space depends above all on the state of the economy and on sound legislation giving all information actors equal rules.

Comparative analysis of Internet use in European Union countries Source

A comparative snapshot of Internet use across the European Union at the turn of the 2000s, built on European Commission statistics from 1999–2001 and framed by the Council of Europe's 1999 Budapest declaration on new information technologies. It compares the member states on citizens' use of government pages, Internet access at schools and universities and searches for medical information, then traces institutional uptake between 1999 and 2001 — users, workplace access, organisations online and intranets — across ten countries. Implementing e-governance amid network warfare

Written as Russia's war against Ukraine was unfolding, the article examines what network warfare does to a state that is simultaneously trying to govern electronically. It identifies the most exposed components of e-government and e-democracy — state information resources and databases, citizens' personal data, including those of residents of the occupied territories and anti-terrorist operation participants, and any electronic service that requires personal identification — and shows how social networks, public polls and some civic organisations can be turned against national security. Its prescription is sequenced: build a national electronic identification system to European eIDAS standards, protect information and personal data, and block the destructive channels, keeping the balance between security and privacy.

How e-governance impacts decentralisation

The paper examines how e-governance relates to decentralisation, with attention to the role of local authorities in delivering public services. The paper places digital tools in the context of responsibilities shared across central and local government. It raises the question of how to coordinate services when responsibilities span several levels.

EGAP 'E-governance for accountability and community participation' (Switzerland)

EGAP is the Swiss-Ukrainian programme ‘E-Governance for Accountability and Participation’, implemented by East Europe Foundation with the support of Switzerland to make government more accountable and to widen citizen participation through digital tools. Its first phase ran from 2015 to 2019. Citizens trust government more when they can see how decisions are made and take part in them. EGAP — 'E-Governance for Accountability and Community Participation' — is a Swiss-Ukrainian programme, run by the East Europe Foundation, that used digital tools to open up government and involve communities. Prof. Svitlana Chukut joined the programme as an expert in November 2015. In its training component (Component 2) — which studied and generalised the best international and national experience and developed the training documentation on that basis, trained trainers and gave methodological and consultative help to those organising and running classes for state servants and local-government officials, and built the capacity of executive bodies, local self-government and citizens to use e-governance and e-democracy tools — her expert task in 2016 was to help create a national training course on e-governance and e-democracy for civil servants and local-government officials. She co-authored the curriculum of an elective university discipline on the subject (the study and work programme texts; 40 hours in total, her personal contribution 20 hours) and prepared ready-to-teach materials for two themes of the course documentation set, each with theory, practical and seminar guidance, test tasks, a glossary and recommended literature: Theme 7, 'Monitoring, evaluation and forecasting of the development of the e-governance system', and Theme 8, 'Development of electronic governance at the regional and local levels', co-authored with V. M. Dreshpak. The final products were delivered to the working-group head and the Component 2 coordinator, so officials across Ukraine get one national course and ready teaching materials on e-governance and e-democracy.

APA 7EGAP programme. (2015–2017). EGAP 'e-governance for accountability and community participation' (switzerland) [Research project].

Modern warfare, the network society and crowd psychology Source

Conference theses applying Serge Moscovici's theory of the crowd to Russia's war against Ukraine in 2013–2014. Prof. Chukut restates the theory's postulates — the crowd as a psychic community acting unconsciously, its conservatism and need of a leader, propaganda's irrational basis, and the role of a higher idea turned into collective images — and shows how Russian propaganda built its "fascist" framing over a decade, from the 2004 campaign to the Revolution of Dignity, the occupation of Crimea and the invasion of the mainland. In a network society, she argues, television, radio, print, online media and social networks act synergistically on mass consciousness through overlay and projection, and simplified, endlessly repeated idea-images ("Kyiv junta", "fascists", "punishers") trigger behaviour automatically. The Maidan, she notes, was not a crowd but a community of like-minded individuals, which is why the weapon failed in Kyiv; as a counter-example she cites Serhiy Loiko's Tolkien imagery ("Mordor", "orcs") in the October 2014 Echo of Moscow interview, removed from the station's site by Roskomnadzor. Modern war, she concludes, is fought with information weapons as much as with armies, and Ukraine can use them offensively as well as in defence.

APA 7Chukut, S. (2014). Modern warfare, the network society and crowd psychology. Plenary talk, 'Great Wars, Great Transformations' Conference, Kyiv. https://sociology.kpi.ua/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/Програма_Соціологія_2014.pdf

E-governance implementation amid network warfare

Conference theses in which Prof. Chukut asks what e-governance becomes under the network war Russia is waging against Ukraine. She recalls the positive steps of 2014 — the creation of the State Agency for E-Governance Development and the draft Green Paper on e-governance in Ukraine — and sets them against the nature of network war as defined by its Russian ideologue Alexander Dugin: destroying a people's fundamental ideas of their culture, society and state so as to sow fear, disorientation and chaos, reorient and then destroy traditional spiritual and cultural values, and establish control without direct occupation, through integrated physical, informational, cognitive and social efforts in which the information component leads. Against this background, she warns, the Green Paper's e-democracy instruments — collecting signatures and petitions, appeals, consultations, questionnaires, electronic voting — can produce the opposite effect: she cites the Le Figaro poll on selling the Mistrals to Russia, falsified by mass automated voting (of some 260,000 respondents, 180,000 came from robot-like IP addresses, most of them Russian). Particular risks attach to electronic interaction between state and local authorities, where IT companies with a "Russian trace" may be involved; to electronic services, which require a national electronic identification system; and to the protection and content of the databases state bodies create. She poses the unresolved balance — state security against privacy, e-democracy's development against victory in the network war — and concludes that Ukraine's task is to use e-governance's advantages for victory while shielding its most vulnerable components from foreign interference: better to move more slowly, but in the right direction.

APA 7Chukut, S. (2014). E-governance implementation amid network warfare. 'V. Hlushkov, Cybernetics Pioneer', Kyiv.

Conferences · 2014 · 'V. Hlushkov, Cybernetics Pioneer', Kyiv

Trends and problems of e-governance implementation in Ukraine

Conference theses in which Prof. Chukut frames e-governance as the answer to a worldwide deficit of trust between citizens and government: the global network creates sustainable feedback and interactive interaction, and e-democracy — a core component of e-governance — serves citizens' needs while countering corruption, bureaucratisation and formalism. She restates the OECD criteria for building e-government and its working principles — services at any time (24/7), maximal simplicity and transparency for ordinary citizens, common technical standards and interoperability, confidentiality and information security, and unconditional orientation to citizens' opinion — and surveys Ukraine's current development: electronic document flow with digital signature, administrative service centres and the "single window", and sectoral e-governance from telemedicine and distance education to the courts. She closes by outlining seven problem blocks: interoperability, national security, national identity, economic security, privacy protection (warning of an Orwellian outcome if personal-data rules fail), responsibility, and force majeure — arguing that the most critical services should keep a 70–80 percent electronic share rather than going fully electronic.

The Impact of E-Governance on Societal Transformations

Can digital government change society for the better — and what gets in the way? From 2013 to 2017, an initiative research theme led by Prof. Svitlana Chukut at the Faculty of Sociology and Law of Kyiv Polytechnic (Department of Theory and Practice of Management) studied that question on three fronts. First, the e-parliament: the team analysed how e-parliament is being introduced in Ukraine against current world trends, checking the structure and completeness of the information on the Verkhovna Rada portal against the recommendations of the Global Centre for ICT in Parliament, and identified the priorities and the problems. An e-parliament is a legislature empowered by ICT to be more open, transparent and accountable, and Ukraine's level matches international trends; the main obstacles are citizens' poor awareness of what the e-parliament offers and weak coordination between the legislative and executive branches. The work also stressed mobile applications — for simpler access to information and services, and for monitoring public opinion. Second, smart cities: the team studied modern approaches to the concepts of 'smart city' and 'e-city' in local e-governance — one approach, promoted by large IT companies, aims at automating all city processes, while the other, set in the frame of sustainable development, uses ICT in every sphere of city life to improve residents' quality of life — and named the threats of excessive enthusiasm for smart-city technologies: risks to privacy, total control over citizens, and the devaluation of citizen participation in decision-making. Third, the local level: Ukrainian and foreign practices of e-governance development at the local level were analysed, the main problems slowing local e-governance in Ukraine were identified, and recommendations for overcoming them were developed. The results were implemented in the teaching process; the theme produced 5 articles in journals indexed in scientometric databases and 5 in professional journals from the list of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine, 22 conference presentations (18 of them at international conferences), involved 17 students, and 10 master's theses were prepared and defended. The results can be used by the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, the State Agency for E-Governance Development, the Ministry of Economic Development, local state administrations and local self-government bodies, and in teaching specialty 074 'Public Administration and Administration'.

Staffing for e-governance implementation

Written with Oleksandr Kukarin and Olha Zahvoiska, the article treats qualified personnel as the precondition for implementing electronic governance. The e-governance master's programme

Prof. Chukut's contribution to the Kyiv collection "Experience in Implementation of E-Democracy and E-Governance in Ukraine" (2010) presents the master's programme in electronic governance developed at the National Academy of Public Administration — the first of its kind in Ukraine, prepared in 2008 for the speciality "Electronic Governance" (8.150110) and approved by Ministry of Education and Science Directive No. 268 of 24 March 2009. The text sets out the programme's goals — training specialists who use modern ICT creatively, introduce advanced e-governance technologies for public services, and improve public administration to world and European standards — the eight professional skills it forms, from drafting strategies and concepts to assessing an institution's electronic readiness, and its distinctive features: strong practical orientation, two-stage traineeship ending in a defended master's thesis, and European training dimensions. It lists the mandatory disciplines, from e-democracy to electronic services, and the four specialisation tracks — national, local and regional, business, and information management.

Research: 'Foundations for e-governance implementation'

Ukraine wanted digital government, but there was no shared playbook for how to build it. Led by Prof. Svitlana Chukut at the National Academy of Public Administration (2010–2011, state registration No. 0201U004833), this project studied the regularities of how e-governance forms and develops in Ukraine and the world, set out its essence, methods and principles, and examined models of its implementation at national, regional and local levels. It studied the problems and prospects of e-governance formation against domestic practice, and the stages and tasks of implementation against best foreign practice — and the team took direct part in drafting the Concept of E-Governance Development in Ukraine. Its products were practical: a methodological guide on introducing e-governance in a general-education school; the methodological materials 'Best practices of e-governance implementation: foreign experience' (2010, 144 pp.); information-analytical materials 'State and problems of e-governance implementation in the central and local executive bodies of Ukraine'; the electronic proceedings of the conference 'Challenges and opportunities of e-governance implementation in a crisis'; and the first two issues of the international scientific journal 'E-Governance'. The results were used by the Secretariat of the Cabinet of Ministers (its information resources and technologies department) and by the State Committee for Informatization, and were embedded in the course 'Theoretical-methodological, organisational and institutional foundations of e-governance' for the master's speciality 'E-Governance'.

Interoperability of e-public service delivery

Written with Olha Zahvoiska for the "Bulletin of the Civil Service of Ukraine" (2009, No. 1), the article argues that interoperability is not a narrow technical question of computer networks: it extends to exchanging information between networks and reorganising administrative procedures so that electronic public services can actually be delivered — across administrations, across levels of government and across the European Union's borders. Uncoordinated development, the authors warn, produces "islands" of e-government that cannot interact. The answer they develop is professional training: after surveying master's programmes in e-governance from Syracuse and McGill to Oslo, Tampere and Waseda, the article presents the first Ukrainian master's programme in e-governance, developed at the National Academy's Information Policy Department in 2008 — its modules, four specialisations and the competencies its graduates were expected to carry into state and local administration.

APA 7Chukut, S., & Zahvoiska, O. (2009). Interoperability of e-public service delivery. Bulletin of the Civil Service of Ukraine, (1), 78–81.
