Research: 'Establishing mechanisms of effective interaction between the Government, the public and the media: theoretical and applied aspect'

Government decisions land better when officials, citizens and the media actually understand each other. Led by Prof. Svitlana Chukut (2009–2010, state registration No. 0109U003027), this research designed practical mechanisms for that interaction — and tested them outside the classroom. The team pilot-tested the level of civic responsibility: through the 'School of e-governance' pilot in Novovorontsovka district, Kherson region, and through a communicative project run under a resolution of the Head of the Council of Ministers of Crimea. It developed and put into practice the sociocultural and information projects 'Civic responsibility' and a video, and developed and implemented, at the Kherson Regional State Administration, the project 'Mechanisms of forming the Presidential personnel reserve "New Elite of the Nation" at the regional level'. Its written products included methodological recommendations for the course 'Communications in public administration' (48 pp.), the scientific-methodical manual 'Establishing mechanisms of the Government's interaction with non-governmental organisations' (64 pp., produced by an author team led by Prof. Chukut), a seminar-training programme on the Government's interaction with NGOs, and the completed textbook 'Communications in public administration'. The uptake was formalised in implementation acts: the Public Relations Department of the Secretariat of the Cabinet of Ministers (December 2009), the Council of Ministers of Crimea (21 January 2010), the Press and Information Department of the Kherson Regional State Administration (15 December 2010) and the Education Department of Novovorontsovka district (22 January 2010). Through her participation in the State Committee for Informatization working group, the work also fed into the Concept of E-Governance Development in Ukraine, adopted by Cabinet Resolution No. 2250-r of 13 December 2010.

Information Policy: a textbook (2nd ed.)

A fundamental study guide offering a comprehensive examination of the theoretical, legal and managerial foundations of information policy in the context of building the information society, integrating the approaches of public administration, political science, law and the theory of strategic communications. Prof. Svitlana Chukut's authorial contribution covers the institutional-managerial and digital blocks of the discipline: the theoretical and methodological foundations of implementing electronic government, the stages of the digital transformation of public administration and the models of electronic democracy; a comparative analysis of successful world practices of information-society and e-governance development (the European Union, the USA, Great Britain, Estonia, Singapore); and the mechanisms of Ukraine's state information policy, the protection of information resources, citizens' access to public information and overcoming the digital divide. One of the first basic academic editions in Ukraine to integrate e-governance into a general course on state information policy, the book contains a complete teaching and methodological complex — a glossary, review questions, topics for research papers and the normative base — and is widely used in training specialists in public administration, political science, international relations and information security.

How should a ministry or a town hall talk with the public — openly, professionally, and especially in a crisis? E-Democracy: essence and main stages Source

Prof. Chukut's paper in the E-Governance Day 2008 proceedings (pp. 89–95). She defines e-democracy as the state ensuring the necessary preconditions for citizens to participate in developing and adopting state decisions with the help of modern information and communication technologies, and explains that e-governance builds the trust between government and citizens on which it rests — through participation in decision-making, openness, accountability and the prevention of corruption. She sets out the main stages of e-democracy's formation: e-informing, a one-way flow from state bodies to citizens (access to documents, catalogues, registers and indexes, published draft laws and white and green papers, online reports and guides, via email, web portals, mobile communication, information kiosks and discs — with the attendant problems of confidential information, state secrets, privacy and national security); e-consultation, in which the government asks citizens' opinion online and receives requests, complaints, proposals and survey answers in a limited two-way relationship hindered by the digital divide; e-participation, citizens' active, feedback-based involvement in decision-making and policy-making through government and public forums and chats, interactive games and virtual workspaces; and e-partnership, in which responsibility for decisions is shared by both sides on a basis of mutual trust — a stage still in its infancy. She closes with the problems to be solved — digital inequality, access for people with disabilities, ICT illiteracy, staffing, technical capacity, financing, legal status and accountability, security and privacy — and the ways to solve them, from ensuring access and re-engineering the civil service to amending legislation and combining ICT with traditional means.

Problems and prospects of e-governance development in the conditions of modern social progress: foreign and domestic experience

How do you bring government online in a country where the idea is still new — and what can be learned from countries that started earlier? In this 2006 research study, Prof. Svitlana Chukut set out to identify and study the problems of e-governance in the modern development of Ukraine and other countries, drawing on their shared experience, and to work out scientifically grounded proposals and recommendations for implementing e-governance and the prospects for its development. The study compared the e-governments of the world's leading countries with the situation in Ukraine, examined the main problems and achievements in the formation of e-government in Ukraine, and weighed the advantages of e-governance alongside traditional administration in order to set the priorities for digital democracy. Its results were new in several respects: fundamentally new definitions of e-government, new approaches to forming e-government in Ukraine divided into stages, and new approaches to overcoming the obstacles in the way. The comparison supported a practical conclusion — Ukraine has all the resources to build an integral e-government system and to involve citizens themselves as the main actors of state policy — and the study closed with practical recommendations, including for the Academy's teaching: new e-governance courses and a specialisation.

Problems and prospects of e-government implementation: world and domestic experience

Prof. Chukut distinguishes the competing terms — e-governance, e-state, e-management, e-society — and defines e-government as the adaptation of public administration to the new requirements of social development: both the services the state provides to citizens and their interactive interaction through a feedback system (citizen → government → citizen) built on modern ICT. She describes the three stages of e-government formation — government websites carrying reference information; integration into a single portal with interactive services and feedback; and predominantly online communication with round-the-clock services and digital democracy — and reports the UN E-Government Survey 2003 readiness index, on which Ukraine (0.462) stood slightly above the world average (0.402) and ahead of Russia and Belarus, while the United States (0.927) led. Ukraine, she argues, lacks both a concept for building the information society and a body responsible for it — unlike Canada's Information Highway Advisory Council, the US Information Infrastructure Task Force or the EU's Directorate-General for Information Society — and she groups the obstacles into financial, technological, mental, cultural, educational, political and professional problems. The article then examines the most widespread problems of e-government implementation and their solutions in the United States (including the four reasons ICT spending failed to raise public-sector productivity, share-in-savings contracts under the E-Government Act of 2002, and measures against the digital divide), the European Union and Great Britain.

The essence of e-government and principles of its organisation

In this early programmatic article, written to open a journal rubric on the essence and development of electronic government, Prof. Chukut examines the contested definitions of e-government — as a portal, as interactive state–citizen interaction (Vershinin), as network information and communication infrastructure (Koshkin) — and the OECD's e-government project with its four assessment groups, from foresight and public-administration reform to measurement. Drawing on the eEurope 2002 and 2005 programmes and the draft "Electronic Ukraine" programme, she distinguishes a government that is merely online from a true electronic government, sets out eleven principles for organising e-government — citizen orientation, convenience and simplicity, business transformation, minimal cost and complexity, service quality, compliance, scalability, performance, reporting, speed of implementation and readiness to act — and concludes with e-government defined as the adaptation of public administration to new conditions of social development, built on a citizen–government feedback loop.

Building the information society in Ukraine: problems and prospects

Prof. Chukut surveys the first steps toward building an information society in Ukraine. After noting the world community's parallel efforts — the eEurope initiative, the United Kingdom's modernising-government programme, Russia's federal "Electronic Russia" programme — she lists the Ukrainian framework created between 1998 and 2003: the Law on the National Informatization Program, presidential decrees on Internet access in Ukraine, on openness of state authorities and on protecting state information resources, Cabinet resolutions on publishing executive activity online and on creating the "Electronic Government" information system (24 February 2003), and the draft "Electronic Ukraine" programme. She concludes that, although the need is fully recognised at the level of state administration, most problems remain unresolved, and closes with the Council of Europe's 1999 Budapest Declaration: a truly democratic information society rests on policies encouraging access and participation, competence and readiness, creativity and diversity with appropriate protection.

State cultural policy amid the information society: foreign and domestic experience

Prof. Chukut examines how the building of the information society transforms state cultural policy, drawing on UNESCO's analysis and European practice. She sets out the four aspects UNESCO identifies: new information technologies generate new communication models and a new aesthetic discourse, feeding "global creativity"; the cultural industry gains economic weight on a global market, sharpening copyright and anti-piracy problems; cultural heritage — material and immaterial — becomes a policy prerogative exposed to illegal trade and transnational actors; and the information revolution itself carries economic, social and political consequences that demand a clear definition of public interests in cyberspace and protection of citizens' rights. She reviews UNESCO's Medium-Term Strategy for 1996–2001 and argues that cultural policy's focus shifts from the creative process itself to the means of transmitting its results to the consumer. Canada's experience — a national information highway centred on culture and the digitisation of heritage, whose support for domestic media production turned the country into a major exporter of film and video — is set against the European Union's: the Fourth Framework Programme, the "Multimedia Access to Europe's Cultural Heritage" Memorandum of Understanding (1995–1998), and the first Culture 2000 programme, with their commitments on digitised access, heritage protection and cultural diversity. She concludes that common features of modern cultural policy — IT in both creation and dissemination, digitised heritage with non-discriminatory access, lifelong distance education, protection of morality and democratic values, preservation of cultural and linguistic diversity, and deeper international cooperation — should be introduced into Ukraine's own cultural policy.

Ethical and cultural dominants of the political process

An article on the ethical and cultural dominants of the political process — tradition, stereotype and ritual as the forms that reproduce the generational integrity of spiritual culture. Prof. Chukut first names the negative moments in the relations between spiritual culture and politics: the domination of the political will to power by spiritless economic forces, its subjection to expansionist nationalism, and the distortion of originally spiritual concepts and of the noble national idea; with Alfred Weber's Germany as example, she ties these to the absence of an old political tradition able to absorb spiritual elements into practice, of that tradition's symbolic embodiment, and of definite guiding ideas pointing to humanity's mission. She then examines each dominant: tradition, which over time can lose adaptability and harden into a stereotype — stable, rigid and conservative, built of a cognitive image and an instrumental-practical attitude, and able in the political process to popularise a phenomenon according to public opinion and those who shape it; and ritual, which following Foucault she sets within politics as activity crystallised by a spiritual culture that is itself a code of conduct. Political ritual draws a magic circle around rulers even as mass media bring their images closer; it fixes legitimacy on a territory by reviving rituals that appeal to national memory and common patriotic values — flag, awards, invocations of the nation in leaders' speeches — thereby expressing the governed's cohesion around shared values, symbols and history and renewing collective approval of established power, as in a new leader's tour of the country. Alongside these consensual rituals stand rituals of confrontation — rallies and street demonstrations, symbols of antagonism that likewise require their supporters' physical presence — and she closes on the modern condition: political ritual is now unthinkable without mass media, above all television, which favours novelty, while ritual itself always sets tradition in motion by direct or hidden reference to it.

Implementing state cultural policy as a priority for the humanitarian sphere

An article arguing that implementing state cultural policy is the priority direction for developing Ukraine's humanitarian sphere. Opening from President Kuchma's address — that economic and social progress depends more on the spiritual and cultural component than on purely technical innovation, and that neglect of the humanitarian sphere has cost the state dearly — Prof. Chukut orders the concepts dialectically: state policy as the general realisation of the state's interests, humanitarian policy as its particular form addressed to citizens and their worldview, and cultural policy as the concrete realisation of the state's interests in culture, where culture is both the result and the means of a person's and a society's self-awareness and self-knowledge; cultural policy must therefore be integrative, spanning all spheres of social life. She defines the state's cultural policy by its first tasks — educating citizens, preserving cultural identity, upholding rituals and norms, and supporting citizens' creative contribution to spiritual culture — in line with UNESCO's definition, and insists that it is wrong to reduce it to either "managing culture" or "supporting culture": both are needed, expressed in clear priorities for what the state manages and funds. Citing Institute of Sociology data (1994–1998) on Ukrainians' shrinking access to their national culture and deteriorating opportunities to take part in cultural life, she faults the metaphysical approach that treats consequences rather than causes and borrows foreign forms uncritically. She then examines the European Union's first culture programme, Culture 2000 — its support for creativity, heritage, cultural diversity and a common European cultural space — within Ukraine's EU-integration strategy, and concludes that Ukraine's cultural policy must learn to answer the challenge of global economic change, drawing on the whole wealth of Ukrainian and world heritage to revive national identity and serve state-building.

Conceptual analysis of choice in managing socio-cultural processes

An article giving a conceptual analysis of choice as the mechanism by which, within continuity, the problem of attaining the ideal is resolved — social choice depending on the level of a society's developed needs. Chukut begins from the existentialist premise (Sartre, Camus) that a person is a self-made project who always chooses, even in catastrophe: submission can itself be conscious. With Lypynsky she holds that conscious choice in political creativity presupposes free will beside innate, spontaneous desires — the highest forms of culture were created by people and nations who believed in free will and chose between good and evil — while a person still inherits the statics of social life: the language, territory, state order and cultural level found at birth, which ease or complicate one's own creativity. Against Althusser's structuralism, in which the person is a puppet of the ideological state apparatus performing pre-written roles, she sets the ethical core of the problem: with Kierkegaard, the absolute choice is between good and evil, and what matters is the act of choosing itself, performed with energy and passion, by which the personality defines itself — delay is itself a loss, for life then chooses in one's stead. Reading Nietzsche's three metamorphoses of the spirit as three types of choice, she maps the camel ("thou shalt", the state choosing for the person) onto formal continuity and the child — the person who consciously chooses from humanity's accumulated heritage or creates what is missing — onto informal continuity, with the lion ("I will") as negation between them; choice thus actualises the content of continuity, and the more developed a society and its needs, the more consciously its choice of continuity is made.

The state idea and the social ideal: their functional role in Ukraine's state-building

An article on the functional role of the state idea and the social ideal in Ukraine's state-building. Prof. Chukut argues that a transforming society needs a single consolidating beginning that gives meaning to change across all spheres: historically this integrative function was performed by state religions (Hinduism in India, Confucianism in China, Protestantism in England) and in the modern world by ideologies such as Marxism-Leninism. She examines how the United States built its American Creed and how Japan — under its samurai elite, which preserved and developed the national culture while deliberately adopting Western technology, institutions and science, and rejecting Western individualism — modernised without losing itself, an experience she judges most useful for Ukraine. Through Ilyenkov, Kant, Marx, Novgorodtsev's absolute ideal and Weber's ideal types she distinguishes the ideal — society's unattainable model of what it strives to be — from the idea, the practical means of approaching it, and, following Franko on Drahomanov, holds that the lack of a national ideal was the chief tragedy of Ukraine's political efforts. Drawing on Tomashevsky's diagnosis of the missing single Ukrainian state idea and on Rymarenko, she traces the idea of an independent, united Ukraine from Cossack autonomy and Khmelnytsky's state through the Ukrainian People's Republic to the 1991 Act of Independence, sets out the state idea's apologetic, critical and futurological functions and the tasks of a state ideology, and proposes as Ukraine's integrating state idea national unity founded on developing its own culture, with critical respect — not blind copying — for the experience of other developed countries.

The essence and role of public opinion in state-building

An article on the essence and role of public opinion in state-building, built largely on Gabriel Tarde's Opinion and the Crowd. Prof. Chukut follows Tarde in distinguishing tradition, reason and public opinion as three branches of the social spirit: opinion develops last but spreads fastest, grows at the expense of the other two, and in modernity has become stronger than both tradition and institutional reason. She traces how individual judgements become public opinion — first through public speech and private conversation, then decisively through the book and above all the periodical press, which welded scattered local opinions into national and even international ones, levelled the weight of voices into a count, awakened national feeling along language borders, and made universal suffrage and parliamentary majority possible, so that power itself is now manufactured in cafés, clubs and salons and transformed by the press that feeds on it. With Hegel's Philosophy of Right she argues that publicity is the most effective means of forming state interests: only through public debate does public opinion gain true content, learn the state's real concerns and come to respect ability and office, while opinion itself — which fuses truth and error, the eternal principles of justice as common sense with prejudice — deserves both respect for its essential ground and contempt for its concrete utterance, and only a great person discerns the true within it. She closes with the public-relations understanding of public opinion as a dynamic consensus arising from coinciding attitudes, its measurable characteristics — direction, intensity, stability, information saturation and social support — and Hadley Cantril's laws of its formation, as the working basis for influencing it.

The creative elite: a theoretical and methodological aspect

A theoretical and methodological article on the creative elite and its place in spiritual culture. Prof. Chukut distinguishes the ruling elite, which decides what citizens should take from humanity's cultural heritage and what artists should create, from the creative elite, which is guided by personal values, creates and activates that heritage, and carries informal continuity — so the direction of continuity in spiritual culture depends on the elite's development, education and professionalism. Through Toynbee she presents civilisation as the work of creative individuals and minorities: the non-creative majority follows by mimesis, imitation directed in primitive societies at the older generation and in civilisations at creative personalities, whose withdrawal-and-return renews them; but mimesis is mechanical, and success breeds the "nemesis of creativity", when yesterday's creators fail the next challenge and block the new — whence the breakdown of civilisations through the creative minority's loss of creativity, the majority's refusal to follow a merely dominant minority, and the loss of social unity. Through Lypynsky she sets out the national aristocracy: the active minority that organises and rules the passive majority, holds material force (the will to power, the means of war and of production) and, indispensably, moral authority grounded in its own public morality and the masses' acceptance. She derives the social mechanism of the creative elite's formation from its functions — bearer of national culture's continuity and of the nation's identity, generator of new knowledge, guide of national revival, participant in the exchange of domestic and world experience, creator of national spiritual culture, guardian of values and historical memory, and driver of the national idea — and closes on the creative personality and the crowd, which mutually define each other: society's level shows in how wide a choice of paths it leaves the person, who may live "parallel" to the crowd by her own rules or confront it "perpendicularly", at the risk of destruction or, through mimesis, of changing social life itself.

Spiritual culture and the national question in Ukraine's state-building

An article on the relationship between spiritual culture and the national question in Ukraine's state-building at the beginning of the twentieth century, when — as in Shevchenko, Kulish, Lesia Ukrainka, Franko, Drahomanov and Hrushevsky — national self-expression became the most pressing question of public life. Following Bochkovsky's development of Mancini, Prof. Chukut sets out culture's threefold significance for a nation: belonging to one cultural type unites a community while marking it off from others; a shared culture — above all language and writing — eases mutual understanding and manifests national belonging; and common cultural interests are a condition of the community's arising. She stresses, with Starosolsky, that historical tradition is not the past itself but the present's living experience of it, and, with Dnistriansky, that a people is constituted by nature, culture and territory, culture being the new factor without which a people does not become a people. Through Mikhnovsky she argues that nationalism is compatible with cosmopolitanism and humanism — save with chauvinism — and that the healthy nationalism of oppressed peoples is a source of creativity and freedom; through Lypynsky, that every nation is a product of history created by its national aristocracy's organisational work, that the statics of social life inherited from previous generations conditions its dynamics, and that political culture grows with accumulated experience, voluntarism and intelligence. She concludes that national self-consciousness, the leading role of the national — ruling and creative — elite, and the link between national culture and state-building remain pressing for state policy in every sphere of Ukraine's life.

What does Ukraine's current ruling elite lack? Source

An article asking what Ukraine's present-day ruling elite lacks. Chukut first separates the ruling elite — which in culture decides what citizens should take from humanity's heritage and what artists should create — from the creative elite, and builds on Lypynsky's national aristocracy: an active minority whose power lasts only when its material force is legitimised by moral authority, itself formed by the aristocracy's public morality and by the masses' acceptance of its forms of organisation; a leading stratum with weak memory, weak conscious will and weak intelligence amid strong emotionality cannot give a nation political culture or a state life of its own. With Toffler she describes the worldwide decay of elites' capacity to take timely, competent decisions, the resulting power vacuum and "black hole" in society, the messianic faith in replacing the leader, and the three fallacies behind the demand for strong leadership — the myth of authoritarian efficiency, the assumption that yesterday's leadership style fits today, and the personalisation of what is in fact institutional collapse — arguing that the Third Wave requires leaders who listen, imagine and accept leadership's limits. For Ukraine, whose ruling elite as that of an independent state is still forming, she presents the 1996–1997 national surveys: the public identifies the elite with the richest (44%) and high office-holders (42%), only 15% with the best and most capable; trust has collapsed (President 17.6%, ministers 2.4%, deputies 3.9%), a third feel resentment or hostility toward the elite and 54% indifference, and Shchokin's profile shows an elite aged mostly 40–50 with predominantly technical education and too few specialists able to run the mechanism of continuity in spiritual culture — hence the irrational use of heritage, the dominance of mass culture and the devaluation of universal values. Against this she sets meritocratic cadre selection (France's National School of Administration, Tokyo University, the US Senior Executive Service; Ukraine's Administrative Reform Commission and the formative role of the Ukrainian Academy of Public Administration) and answers her title directly: what the ruling elite lacks is a single consolidating state idea — as the American Creed in the United States or, in Japan, the samurai elite's union of Eastern spirituality with Western technology, whose targeted modernisation preserved and even strengthened Japanese culture.

The Genesis of Spiritual Culture (the Management Dimension)

Prof. Chukut's monograph (Ukrainian Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine, Kyiv, 1999; approved for publication by the Academy's Academic Council on 24 December 1998) studies the genesis of spiritual culture through the lens of public administration. Written at the turn of the millennium, it opens from the era's spiritual-culture problems — the devaluation of universal values, "creativity to order" measured by money and media accompaniment, the dominance of mass culture, the loss of trust in society's ideals, and the tension between uncritical borrowing of foreign culture and one-sided use of the national heritage. The first chapter traces the mutual conditioning of spiritual culture and state administration from the Ancient world through Hobbes ("the state as a precondition of culture") and Locke ("tradition and civil society"), German classical philosophy and the dialectical-materialist conception of history to the management of cultural continuity in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The second develops a methodology of continuity (succession): spiritual culture as a phenomenon of social life, its continuity characteristics and research methods, its subjects — the ruling elite as the subject of formal continuity and the creative elite of informal continuity — and its mechanisms, in which the ideal is the goal, choice the driver, and public opinion and values the medium. The third examines the forms of continuity — tradition as the principal form, the stereotype as its rudiment, innovation, ritual, habitus, archetype and symbol, and language as the transitional link between forms and means, including the language of politicians and its functioning in contemporary Ukrainian society. The fourth turns to the means: cultural heritage, social institutions and technical means, above all mass media and the computer production of information, within a national system of mass communication. An afterword draws the conclusions into state cultural policy — the support and management of culture.

Spiritual culture in Ukraine's humanitarian policy

A scientific and methodological development prepared at the Ukrainian Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine (Kyiv, 1999), setting out how spiritual culture figures in Ukraine's humanitarian policy. Its first part places culture within state-building: culture as a society's unwritten beliefs, evaluations and accepted rules — analysed through technology, economy, social organisation, religion and symbolism — and spiritual culture not as a frozen result but as the process of creating, accumulating, transmitting and using cultural acquisitions, whose core mechanism is continuity, the reproduction of a generation's cultural integrity. The second part examines Ukraine's state cultural policy: against the command-administrative concept of "managing culture", which subordinated culture to politics and economics, it sets the concept of "supporting culture" recognised by developed democracies and grounded in culture's intrinsic value, while arguing that the cultural sphere reaches far beyond the arts — to education, science, freedom of conscience and of speech — as in UNESCO's definition of cultural policy as the sum of a society's conscious actions aimed at cultural goals. The third part works through nine directions of state policy in spiritual culture: legislative support, the information sphere, cultural heritage, language policy, rituals, ceremonies and holidays, the development of the cultural and artistic sphere, the cultures of national minorities, youth culture, and international cooperation — with the Ministry of Culture and Arts as the central executive body implementing policy in the field.

The impact of state policy on the functioning of spiritual culture continuity forms

An article examining how state policy shapes the functioning of the forms of continuity in spiritual culture — traditions, customs, innovations, rituals, stereotypes, laws and language — through which a society's social and historical experience is accumulated and transmitted. Prof. Chukut defines state policy in culture as the set of the state's goals in the cultural sphere, the principles it observes and the mechanisms that secure them, and takes tradition as the principal form of continuity: passing through formation, intensive development and decline, it accumulates the value-laden experience of past generations, while the stereotype is a tradition frozen and stripped of self-development, and innovation is continuity's external form that renews tradition's outward shapes. Drawing on Unamuno's "eternal tradition", Hayek and Laszlo's critique of modernism, she argues that cultural diversity is humanity's reserve of adaptation, and that state policy acts directly on which forms flourish: where the state creates conditions for a free economy, citizens' free choice and political freedom, innovation is activated first — a pattern recurring roughly every thirty years in Ukraine's spiritual culture, in the late 1920s, late 1950s and late 1980s thaws. She warns that mass and pop culture dehumanise, narrowing a person to material needs, and concludes that spiritual culture forms relatively independent thinking and citizenship, while the national idea produced by the state integrates citizens around a common future and shared values.

Hobbes's theory of the state as a precondition of culture in the context of Ukraine's democratisation

An article reading Thomas Hobbes's theory of the state as a precondition of culture against the problems of democratising Ukrainian society. Prof. Chukut notes that managing continuity in spiritual culture has always stood at the centre of state-building, and presents Hobbes as an early theorist of that control — and of alienation: people create the state, the "great Leviathan", by alienating much of their natural rights, whereupon it rises above its creators and rules them. For Hobbes, outside the state reign the passions, war, fear, poverty and barbarism; within it, reason, peace, security, wealth, the sciences and goodwill — only in the state is there a common measure of virtue and vice, namely its laws, and good dispositions reduce to justice and mercy. She follows his treatment of the instruments of control: religion, historically the first mechanism of state supervision over what people should believe, do and inherit — yet religion, for Hobbes, is not philosophy but law in each state; books and preachers that glorify tyrannicide breed Ravaillacs and Clements rather than citizens; and the sovereign holds the right to judge which doctrines are hostile to civil peace and to forbid them, above all doctrines of divided obedience, the root — she stresses with Hobbes — of every civil war in the Christian world. At the same time she draws out the limits Hobbes sets on power: freedom as the absence of impediments, the distinction between the people (one will, capable of one action) and the multitude, the rule that laws should pursue errors rather than the erring — since opinions are changed by persuasion, not threats — that sound civil doctrine must be codified and taught first in the universities, that rulers sin against their office by multiplying laws beyond the good of the state and its citizens, and that punishment should direct the will rather than break it. She concludes that studying and putting into practice such European experience is necessary for Ukraine's further democratisation.

Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management» · bachelor's · «Administrative Management / E-Governance» programmes4 ECTSElectivePeriodically reviewed and updated

An elective course of the «Administrative Management / E-Governance» programmes (Years 3–4, spring semester; 120 hours, 4 ECTS). It forms students' knowledge and skills in applying communication mechanisms within management activity — in particular to ensure the openness and transparency of public authorities — where a communication campaign is a purposeful attempt to change a target audience's behaviour through organised communication involving the media, social networks and interpersonal interaction. Working in teams, students choose a topical problem, prepare a detailed campaign scenario and actually run the campaign, testing diverse tools and modern ICT. The topics include communication methods, forms and channels, fakes and countering them, social networks and blogs, successful campaign experience abroad and in Ukraine, and the challenges, threats and risks of campaigns.

Doctor of Philosophy programme · Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management»4 ECTSElectivePeriodically reviewed and updated

An elective course of the «Public Management and Administration» programme (Year 2, spring semester; 120 hours, 4 ECTS). It forms doctoral students' knowledge and skills in applying communication mechanisms within management activity — in particular to ensure the openness and transparency of public authorities — covering communication strategies and campaigns, communication channels, campaign planning, work with stakeholders and evaluation of campaign effectiveness. The topics include fakes and countering disinformation, social networks and blogs, drawing up a campaign scenario, and successful campaign experience in foreign countries and in Ukraine, together with the challenges and threats of running campaigns. Each doctoral student develops recommendations for a communication campaign aligned with the topic of their own dissertation research.

Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management» · master's · «Public Administration and E-Governance» programme4 ECTSElectiveDeveloped 2025

An elective course of the «Public Administration and E-Governance» programme (Year 1; 120 hours, 4 ECTS). It forms students' knowledge and skills in developing and applying communication strategies within management activity and business. The topics cover the varieties of communication strategies and their use in public administration and business, communication methods, forms and channels, work with stakeholders, surveys and crafting key messages, social networks and blogs, and fakes and countering them. Students prepare a detailed strategy scenario, study successful foreign experience and the best Ukrainian examples, and learn to evaluate a strategy's effectiveness and to identify risks and prevent them. The course culminates in the team implementation of a communication strategy the students have developed.

Course content

  • Communications diagnostics
  • Stakeholders and channels
  • Strategy: goals, messages, content plan
  • Crisis communications
  • Measuring effectiveness
Specialty 8.15010011 «Electronic Governance» · master's · «Information Management in the E-Governance System» specialisation4 ECTSRequired courseDeveloped 2015

A required course module of the professional and practical training cycle of the Master's specialty 8.15010011 «Electronic Governance», specialisation «Information Management in the E-Governance System» (Year 1, Semester 2; 120 hours, 4 ECTS), assessed by an oral credit, with a creative work as the individual assignment. It forms students' modern theoretical and practical knowledge, skills and abilities in applying communication mechanisms within management activity, ensuring the openness and transparency of public authorities. Its subject is communications within public administration bodies, communications between them, and communications between public authorities and the public. The programme comprises four topics: communications and communicative links in public administration — their concepts, types and legal foundations in Ukraine; intra-organisational communication — individual and group forms, meetings and management styles; the regional aspect of communications — vertical and horizontal links between central and local authorities, and between state power and local self-government; and communications as a democratic mechanism — public consultations and public councils, coverage of authorities' activities, agreements with non-state institutions and forms of local democracy. Students learn to prepare press releases, press conferences and briefings, to work with citizens' appeals and information requests, and to use the Internet for communication with the public, drawing also on international experience of communications in public administration, including in the institutions of the European Communities.

Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management» · master's · «E-Governance» specialisation3 ECTSRequired courseDeveloped 2017

A required course module of the discipline «E-Governance and E-Democracy» of the Master's specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management», specialisation «E-Governance» (Year 1, Semester 2; 90 hours, 3 ECTS), assessed by an examination, with a creative work as the individual assignment. It forms students' theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for the creative use of modern domestic approaches to e-governance and e-democracy, aimed at improving the public administration system itself and fostering innovation processes in society on the basis of world standards. Its subject is the domestic experience of implementing e-governance and e-democracy. The programme comprises nine topics: the information-society development strategy in Ukraine; the main stages of e-governance development in Ukraine; the structure and functions of e-governance across the sectors of public administration; e-democracy and e-governance under network warfare; the development of e-democracy and its main components in Ukraine; the normative-legal support of e-governance and e-democracy in Ukraine; e-democracy tools; electronic services; and the communication campaign, identifying topical e-governance problems. Practical classes are also held in state authorities and local self-government bodies and as a business game; in the creative work, students continue their analysis of a foreign country's experience and compare it with the development of e-governance and e-democracy in Ukraine.

Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management» · bachelor's · «E-Governance» programme · Year 25 ECTSMandatoryDeveloped 2025

A compulsory discipline of the «E-Governance» educational-professional programme in specialty 281 (Year 2, semester 2; 150 hours, 5 ECTS; final assessment — an examination and a coursework paper), taught in full-time and part-time forms. It forms students' ability to solve complex specialised tasks and practical problems of e-democracy and e-participation, applying theories and scientific methods under conditions of complexity and uncertainty. Students learn to build communication between citizens and state and local self-government authorities, to use e-governance and e-democracy technologies and tools, and to research and adapt the best domestic and foreign e-democracy practices to society's development needs. The topics cover an introduction to e-democracy; the essence and main stages of its development; e-participation and its main models; e-democracy tools; e-democracy at the local level; participatory budgets; e-voting; and e-democracy and threats under network warfare. Teaching combines active and collective learning strategies — team-based learning, think-pair-share, brainstorming, case studies, business games and discussions — with heuristic methods and problem-based learning. Working in teams, students develop the project «Propose Your Own!» («Запропонуй своє!») — a project prepared for a participatory-budget competition; the final assignment is a coursework paper with a mandatory public defence.

Specialty 074 «Public Administration and Management» · master's · «Administrative Management» specialisation4 ECTSElectiveDeveloped 2016

A credit module by students' choice of the professional and practical training cycle of the Master's specialty 074 «Public Administration and Management», specialisation «Administrative Management» (Year 1, Semester 2; 120 hours, 4 ECTS), assessed by a differentiated credit, with a creative work as the individual assignment. It forms students' modern theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for the creative use of modern information technologies and the introduction of advanced communication technologies in the interaction of state authorities and local self-government with the public — to engage citizens in developing and making management decisions and to develop civil society, in line with world and European standards. Its subject is the theoretical foundations, methodological approaches and practical skills concerning the foundations of e-democracy, the foreign and domestic experience of its development, and the application of modern electoral technologies. The programme comprises three content modules: the theoretical-methodological and organisational foundations of e-democracy — an introduction to e-democracy and the foundations of e-governance, e-democracy under network warfare, the essence of e-democracy and its components, citizens' e-participation in management decision-making, e-democracy tools (e-appeals, e-petitions, state e-service portals, e- and mobile voting, online participation in urban planning, e-consultations) and the e-parliament in Ukraine and the world; electoral technologies — information electoral technologies as the core component of election campaigns, and their main types and forms of implementation, from educational and image technologies to manipulative ones and the means of countering them; and the electronic communication campaign, planned and conducted by the students as a business game. The legal framework for the development of e-democracy in Ukraine runs through the course.

Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management» · master's · «Public Administration and E-Governance» programme · Year 14 ECTSMandatoryPeriodically reviewed and updated

A mandatory discipline of the «Public Administration and E-Governance» educational programme in specialty 281 (Year 1, autumn semester; 120 hours, 4 ECTS; final assessment — an examination). It forms students' theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for the creative use of modern foreign approaches to e-governance and e-democracy, aimed at improving the public administration system itself and fostering innovation processes in society on the basis of world standards. Built on the principle of constructive alignment and a student-centred approach, the syllabus requires each successive task to draw on the skills and knowledge gained in the previous one. The topics run from e-government to smart governance; the UN reports on e-governance development abroad; implementation in Ukraine; electronic services; the essence of e-democracy and its main components; e-voting; the e-parliament; and e-governance and e-democracy under network warfare. Students learn to set priority directions for e-governance implementation and e-democracy development, to use e-democracy tools drawing on the best foreign experience, and to research a topical implementation problem independently. The final assignments are a team project and an individual creative work with a mandatory public defence. Teaching the course, the author developed and introduced her own educational innovation practice «Master it, research it, implement it!» («Опануй, досліди, впровадь!»), which won a prize at the All-Ukrainian competition «Best Practices for Introducing Educational Innovations in the System of Professional Training of Civil Servants, Heads of Local State Administrations, Their First Deputies and Deputies, Local Self-Government Officials and Deputies of Local Councils», organised by the National Agency of Ukraine on Civil Service, in the nomination «Training of Master's Students in Specialty 281 Public Administration and Management» (2020).

Specialty 8.15010011 «Electronic Governance» · master's · «Information Management in the E-Governance System» specialisation4 ECTSMandatoryDeveloped 2015

A compulsory (normative) course of the Master's specialty 8.15010011 «Electronic Governance», specialisation «Information Management in the E-Governance System» (Year 1; 120 hours, 4 ECTS). It forms students' modern theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for the creative use and introduction of advanced information and communication technologies across the sectors of e-governance, thereby fostering innovation in society and raising the effectiveness of public administration. The course treats information-technology means as an integral component of e-governance: the concept of a unified architecture and information-technological infrastructure of e-governance, the components of that infrastructure, information resource systems, and the foundations of software and technical support. Students learn to define the architecture and information-technological infrastructure of e-governance in line with state functions, to build architectures of information resources, applied systems and common services, and to organise information management in e-governance. The discipline is also taught at bachelor's level, under the 2018 working programme written for the educational-professional programme «E-Governance» of specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management» (field 28): a mandatory discipline of 5.5 ECTS credits (165 hours, in full-time and part-time forms), assessed by an examination. Its subject is e-governance systems and the foreign and domestic experience of implementing them; it forms students' ability to solve complex specialised tasks and practical problems of e-governance architecture. The bachelor's programme comprises five topics: the main elements of e-governance architecture — the components of e-government, the telecommunication environment, interagency interaction systems, the electronic identification and authorisation infrastructure and the applied systems behind e-services, with world experience and the architecture of e-governance systems in Ukraine; the theoretical and normative-legal foundations of using Internet of Things technologies in e-governance, including personal-data protection; the theoretical and technological foundations of smart-city development; the use of Big Data and open data in e-governance systems; and the monitoring and assessment of the e-readiness of state authorities and local self-government bodies — tested in a business game and a team project assessing the e-readiness of a chosen institution.

Specialty 074 «Public Administration and Management» · master's · «E-Governance» specialisation5 ECTSMandatoryDeveloped 2016

A mandatory (normative) course of the «E-Governance» specialisation (180 hours, 5 credits). It forms students' theoretical and practical knowledge for the creative use and implementation of modern e-governance methods — its development patterns in Ukraine and the world, its essence, methods and principles — aimed at improving the public administration system on the basis of world standards. The subject is state policy and the theoretical-methodological, normative, organisational and institutional foundations of e-governance: information-society development strategy, concepts and models of e-governance, foreign experience and implementation in Ukraine, institutions, the legal framework, and electronic services. The topics conclude with the structure and functions of e-governance across the sectors of public administration and a team communication campaign on a topical e-governance problem.

Doctor of Philosophy programme · Specialty 074 «Public Administration and Management»4 ECTSElectiveDeveloped 2016

A Doctor of Philosophy course of the professional training cycle, aimed at the universal competencies of a researcher (120 hours, 4 credits). It forms doctoral students' theoretical and practical knowledge for the creative use and implementation of modern e-governance methods, aimed at improving the public administration system itself and fostering innovation in society on the basis of world standards. The course shares the programme's core sequence — information-society development strategy, concepts, principles and models of e-governance, foreign experience and implementation in Ukraine, institutions, the legal framework and electronic services — and gives it a sectoral focus: the structure and functions of e-governance across the sectors (branches) of public administration, including e-services in foreign countries and electronic administrative services in Ukraine. Specialty 8.15010011 «Electronic Governance» · master's · «Information Management in the E-Governance System» specialisation4 ECTSRequired courseDeveloped 2015

A required course module of the professional and practical training cycle of the Master's specialty 8.15010011 «Electronic Governance», specialisation «Information Management in the E-Governance System» (Semester 1; 120 hours, 4 ECTS), assessed by an oral examination, with a creative work as the individual assignment. It forms students' theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for the creative use and introduction of modern e-governance methods and information and communication technologies in the system of providing state and municipal electronic services. The programme covers the essence and classification of electronic services; the systems of state services and of municipal services — their standards, regulations and catalogues; information management in the electronic-services system; the experience of organising electronic service provision in leading countries of the world; and the normative-legal support for electronic services in Ukraine. Students learn to coordinate the creation and functioning of an electronic-services system, to apply the basic technologies of providing electronic services, to organise information management within it, and to organise citizens' access to electronic services.

Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management» · master's · «E-Governance» specialisation2 ECTSRequired courseDeveloped 2017

A required course module of the discipline «E-Governance and E-Democracy» of the Master's specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management», specialisation «E-Governance» (Year 1, Semester 1; 60 hours, 2 ECTS), assessed by a differentiated credit, with a creative work as the individual assignment. It forms students' theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for the creative use of modern foreign approaches to e-governance and e-democracy, aimed at improving the public administration system itself and fostering innovation processes in society on the basis of world standards. The module is delivered in full-time and part-time forms of study. Its subject is the foreign experience of implementing e-governance and e-democracy. The programme comprises nine topics: information-society development strategy; the concept, principles, methods and models of e-governance; the main models and approaches to implementing e-governance in foreign countries, on the example of the EU — the «eEurope» programme and the European e-government action plans; institutions in e-governance; electronic services; the essence of e-democracy and its components; the normative-legal support of e-governance and e-democracy; citizens' e-participation in management decision-making; and the e-parliament. In the creative work, each student analyses in depth the e-governance experience of one of the UN's top-50 e-government countries and formulates conclusions and recommendations on applying that experience in Ukraine.

Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management» · bachelor's · «Administrative Management» programme5 ECTSRequired courseDeveloped 2024

A required course of the «Administrative Management» programme (Year 2, spring semester; 150 hours, 5 ECTS). It forms students' knowledge of the foundations and current trends of e-governance and e-democracy — the G2G, G2C, G2B and G2E interaction models, the stages of e-governance development and the UN EGDI index — and of identifying the challenges and threats that arise in implementation. Doctor of Philosophy programme · Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management»5 ECTSRequired courseDeveloped 2025

A required course of the Doctor of Philosophy programme «Public Management and Administration» in specialty 281 (Year 2, autumn semester; 150 hours, 5 ECTS). It builds doctoral students' theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for the creative use and implementation of modern e-governance and digital-governance technologies and tools — including artificial intelligence — aimed at improving the public administration system itself and fostering innovation processes in society in line with world standards. Its subject is the study of the strategic directions of e-governance development: current trends, technologies and methodologies, including AI, digital tools and innovative practices. The fourteen webinars and their hands-on workshops cover an introduction to e-governance and digital governance; development trends — mobile, digital and smart governance; AI in public administration — opportunities and challenges; international e-governance indices — methodology and assessment; current trends in e-democracy; e-governance and smart cities — strategies, plans and indices; e-voting — challenges and threats; the Diia platform's role in Ukraine's digital transformation; crisis-oriented digital governance in emergencies (war and pandemics); priority directions from the best international and Ukrainian practices; ethics and data privacy in digital governance; and future trends — AI, blockchain and beyond. The course culminates in team presentations of the e-governance development strategies the doctoral students have developed.

Doctor of Philosophy programme · Specialty 281 «Public Administration and Management» · Year 27 ECTSMandatoryDeveloped 2021

A required course of the third (educational-scientific) level of higher education, within the educational programme «Public Management and Administration» of specialty 281 (field 28 «Public Management and Administration») (Year 2, autumn semester; 210 hours, 7 ECTS). Its aim is to combine scholarly research with practice: each doctoral student follows an individual working programme of the practice, formed in line with the topic of their dissertation research and from the tasks of pedagogical, educational, methodological and organisational work at the department. Doctoral students deepen their knowledge of higher-education pedagogy, carry out scholarly-methodical analysis of course programmes, draw up lesson plans, conduct different kinds of classroom sessions, improve bachelor's and master's disciplines with an author's approach and test their dissertation materials. Taking part in lectures, seminars, conferences, round tables and research circles develops leadership potential, oratorical skills and communication culture. The content comprises six sections: pedagogical activity; methodological activity; research activity; educational activity; organisational activity; and independent work. Semester assessment comprises drawing up the individual working programme and defending the practice report.

Specialty 8.15010011 «Electronic Governance» · master's · «Information Management in the E-Governance System» specialisation4 ECTSRequired courseDeveloped 2015

A required course module of the professional and practical training cycle of the Master's specialty 8.15010011 «Electronic Governance», specialisation «Information Management in the E-Governance System» (Year 1, Semester 1; 120 hours, 4 ECTS), assessed by a coursework project and an oral examination. It forms students' theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for the creative use and introduction of modern e-governance methods and public administration methods aimed at improving the public administration system itself and fostering innovation processes in society on the basis of world standards — using modern information and advanced communication technologies in forming electronic state power, to provide public services to citizens, improve the functioning of the civil service and develop e-democracy. The programme comprises three content modules: the theoretical-methodological foundations of e-governance (its concept, essence and concepts, and foreign implementation experience); the organisational foundations (sectoral e-governance and its normative-legal support); and institutions in e-governance (electronic state power and the electronic institution). Students learn to assess an institution's e-readiness, to develop e-governance strategies for a sector, a territory or a public administration body, to draft legislative and normative acts regulating e-governance implementation, and to adapt foreign experience to Ukraine.

Information policy and e-governance · 2000–2009

Courses Developed at the National Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine

At the Chair of Information Policy, Prof. Svitlana Chukut developed courses and co-developed distance-learning programmes. She also taught in professional development programmes for civil servants and local government officials.

The Academy’s mandate

Accountable to the President of Ukraine, the Academy was the lead state higher education institution in the national system for training civil servants and local government officials. It prepared officials for roles in state and local authorities and provided retraining and continuing professional development. The Cabinet of Ministers regulated admissions, placements and graduate employment.

The Academy’s mandate also covered expert advice and policy analysis. Its regulations prioritised research commissioned by the President and the Cabinet of Ministers and provided for coordination with the presidential administration, known as the Presidential Secretariat during part of this period, on public-service training needs.

The Academy also had special staffing arrangements. Certain management and specialist positions with administrative or advisory duties were classified as civil-service posts.

Regulatory framework at the time
  • Presidential Decree No. 850/2001 — status and mandate
  • Presidential Order No. 168/95-rp — staffing arrangements
  • Cabinet Resolution No. 700 (1995) — civil-service posts
  • Cabinet Resolution No. 468 (2004) — admissions, placements and employment
  • Presidential Decree No. 1445/2005 — establishment of the Presidential Secretariat

Courses and modules with documented syllabi

Specialty 8.150110 «E-Governance» · specialisation level · Year 2, Semester 34 ECTSDeveloped 2009

A specialisation-level course of specialty 8.150110 «E-Governance» at the National Academy's Chair of Information Policy (Year 2, Semester 3; 120 hours, 4 ECTS), taught by Prof. Svitlana Chukut with Olha Zahvoiska and Oleksandr Kukarin. It forms students' theoretical and practical knowledge and skills for the creative use of modern information and advanced communication technologies in building electronic state power — to provide public services to citizens, improve the functioning of the civil service, develop e-democracy and transform the public administration system as Ukraine's information society is built, in line with world and European standards. The topics cover the essence and structure of electronic state power — the electronic parliament, electronic government, electronic justice and the electronic public service — foreign experience of building it, the organisational, legal and institutional foundations of the e-parliament, the institutional models and legal frameworks of e-government, the organisation of e-justice, and the interaction between the components of electronic state power.

Specialty 8.150110 «E-Governance» · master's · required course5 ECTSDeveloped 2009

A required course of the Master's programme in specialty 8.150110 «E-Governance» at the National Academy's Chair of Information Policy (150 hours, 5 credits), compiled by Prof. Svitlana Chukut and Olha Zahvoiska. It forms students' modern theoretical and practical knowledge and skills in state information policy and e-governance, and in establishing effective communications, preparing them for cooperation and interaction in the information society. The programme comprises two modules: «Public Administration and State Policy in the Developing Information Society: Ukrainian and Foreign Experience» (90 hours, 3 credits) — the conceptual foundations of public administration in the information society, state information policy in Ukraine and the world with its legal frameworks and organisational and institutional support, and foreign strategies of information-policy development; and «Communications and Cooperation in the Information Society» (60 hours, 2 credits).

KPI’s official specialty 281 catalogue

Teaching methods and assessment

From concepts to professional decisions

  • “Master, Explore, Implement” structures learning in three steps. Students first learn the concepts, then investigate a case and use the evidence to justify a decision or propose a solution.
  • In SMART CITY: FUTURE – TODAY and CHANGE FOR THE BETTER, learners use simulations to explore stakeholder perspectives and practise decision-making in public management.
  • In Fundamentals of E-Governance, students developed communication campaigns for KPI’s electronic campus and examined how practices from other universities could inform improvements at KPI.

Online and blended course design

Prof. Chukut developed more than ten online and blended courses at KPI. Four Moodle courses received distance-learning certification: Smart Cities, Fundamentals of E-Governance, E-Democracy, and E-Governance and E-Democracy.

At George Brown Polytechnic, Prof. Chukut contributed to 17 course initiatives and more than 50 applied learning modules. Her work included simulations, branching scenarios and assessments aligned with learning outcomes and workplace requirements.

Prof. Chukut uses Moodle and Brightspace (D2L) for online and blended learning, integrating interactive H5P activities and explicit assessment criteria while addressing AODA and WCAG accessibility requirements.

National standards and quality assurance

As chair of Ukraine’s Ministry of Education and Science subcommission on Public Governance and Administration (2016–2019), Prof. Chukut helped lead development of national standards for bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral study. At KPI, she helped align programmes with these standards and contributed to licensing, accreditation and programme review.

View the work on national standards

How the e-governance master’s programme took shape

The National Academy’s planning diagram and its letter to the head of Ukraine’s Main Civil Service Department show how demand from public institutions informed a practice-oriented master’s programme in Electronic Governance. Prof. Chukut’s departmental report records that she initiated the programme in 2008 and led its launch in 2009.

Mandate and stakeholder support
The Academy’s letter cited Presidential Decree No. 474/2006 and the Presidential Secretariat’s letter of 21 April 2008 (No. 02-02/1418). The planning diagram linked the programme to the recommendations of the 2008 E-Governance Day and recorded support from the Main Civil Service Department, the Association of Ukrainian Cities, Brovary City Council and Ukraine’s e-business association.
Two stages of field practice
Students would first gather evidence in a public authority, region or city and design an e-governance project. They would then implement the project and defend a master’s thesis with proposals for resolving the problem they had studied.
Proposed intake and teaching resources
The plan proposed 25 places per study format (daytime, evening and correspondence), with 20 state-funded and five fee-paying places in each. It identified nine department faculty members, specialist practitioners and a planned 25-workstation classroom.
Recognition of the specialty
The Academy’s first vice-president, Oleksandr Obolenskyi, asked Main Civil Service Department head Tymofii Motrenko to consider adding e-governance to the occupational classifier. The letter referred to the qualification profile and educational and professional programme prepared by the Academy.

Presidential Decree No. 474/2006

Sustainable Tourism

Builds on Modules 1 and 2 by comparing sustainable tourism practices at local and global scales and exploring how destinations turn those ideas into practical, balanced, place-specific strategies. Sustainable tourism can fail in two ways: it can stay too broad, using global sustainability language without turning it into action, or too narrow, addressing local issues one by one without linking them to wider goals, standards, or clear measures of progress; strong practice connects broad guidance to local realities. A scenario snapshot follows a small heritage waterfront destination that depends heavily on tourism — its historic core, local food culture, and waterfront events — where peak periods bring crowded public spaces, increased waste, and residents' discomfort, and whose leaders seek practical local solutions, such as better visitor flow, improved transport, stronger local procurement, and protection of culturally sensitive places, while using international standards and destination tools to guide decisions and measure progress. The module's central question: how can a destination use global sustainability guidance without losing local relevance, and how can it combine environmental, socio-cultural, and economic priorities into one workable strategy?

Module outline

3.1. Introduction 3.2 Comparing Local and Global Sustainable Tourism Practices 3.3 Integrating the Environmental, Socio-Cultural, and Economic Aspects of Sustainable Tourism in a Sustainable Tourism Strategy 3.4 Developing and Evaluating a Sustainable Tourism Strategy

Learning outcomes

By the end of this module, you will be able to: Compare and contrast local versus global sustainable tourism practices.

Publication · IPAC · 2026

“Finding Familiar Questions in a New Country”

At IPAC's 2026 National Public Service Symposium in Ottawa, Prof. Svitlana Chukut reflected alongside two fellow Ukrainian professionals on governing in a new country. Her piece opens with a question that runs through more than 25 years of her work where public administration, research and higher education meet: What do we do when technology moves faster than government? She recalls contributing to Ukraine's National E-Governance Concept, adopted in 2010, and initiating the E-Governance Days of 2008–2011, whose 2011 programme engaged more than 1,000 participants. Her current research addresses AI skills among public servants, digital inclusion and digital services during wartime, while at George Brown Polytechnic her curriculum and instructional-design work spans 17 course initiatives and more than 50 practical learning modules — and since 2024, IPAC's own AI training programs have connected her to Canada's public administration community. Her conclusion: governments do not need to chase every technological advance; they need to prepare people, build trust, and make thoughtful decisions when answers are uncertain.

27.08.2021
Initiator, organiser and moderator

All-Ukrainian Seminar on Revising the List of Fields of Study and Specialties

Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute · Online via Zoom

Prof. Svitlana Chukut initiated, organised and moderated this national seminar convened by Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute. Experts, researchers and educators in Public Governance and Administration examined a draft resolution of Ukraine’s Cabinet of Ministers to amend the national list of fields of study and specialties for higher education. They also reviewed the International Standard Classification of Education Fields of Education and Training (ISCED-F 2013), published by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics.

Holding a Doctor of Sciences in Public Administration, Prof. Chukut was a professor in the Department of Theory and Practice of Management. She chaired Subcommission 281 of the Scientific and Methodological Council of Ukraine’s Ministry of Education and Science (2016–2019) and served as deputy chair of Sectoral Expert Council No. 28 at the National Agency for Higher Education Quality Assurance (2019–2020).

Read about ISCED-F 2013 (UNESCO) View the seminar photo
18–19.05.2021
Initiator, organiser and jury chair

First Open University Student Olympiad in E-Governance

Prof. Svitlana Chukut initiated and organised the 18–19 May 2021 Olympiad at Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute and chaired its jury. The online event was open to students from any discipline. The individual competition attracted 69 registrations from 19 institutions, and seven teams from six institutions competed.

Competition design

Combining an olympiad, a hackathon and workshops, the format used tests to assess disciplinary knowledge and case assignments to assess its application. Doctoral students mentored teams. Submissions were anonymised using two levels of coding, and an external observer supported impartial assessment.

Public-sector challenges

The Ministry of Digital Transformation and the EGAP programme contributed practical assignments. One ministry challenge examined how administrative processes could be redesigned for online service delivery. The Ministry of Reintegration’s challenge addressed access to official websites and digital services from temporarily occupied territories.

Educational value and recognition

The workshops covered e-democracy, AI, public service design and youth participation. Winning teams were offered internship opportunities at partner ministries. Ukraine’s National Agency on Civil Service documented the Olympiad as an educational innovation and awarded KPI second place in the relevant 2021 master’s training category.

2011

29.09.2011
Round-table speaker

Towards a Smart Society: Information Technology as a Driver of Social Change in Ukraine

Focus of the contributionHuman-centred digital government

National Institute for Strategic Studies (NISS), Kyiv

As head of the Academy’s Department of Information Policy, Prof. Svitlana Chukut argued that technology should serve human and social development. She cited Estonia’s decision to build its digital strategy around everyday needs and called for Ukraine to combine online government services with e-democracy so that people can participate in decisions and interact with public authorities.

She noted that strong technology indicators do not resolve social challenges. She highlighted children’s exposure to harmful online content as mobile internet access grew, alongside questions about access to personal data, biometric passports and critical IT infrastructure.

11.04.2011 · 17:00
Guest speaker

Chamber IT Committee Meeting

TalkE-Government Days

Chamber Conference Facility, Horizon Park Business Center, 12 Amosova Street, 15th floor, Kyiv

The IT Committee of the American Chamber of Commerce in Ukraine discussed the upcoming E-Government Days, scheduled for 16–20 May by the National Academy of Public Administration under the President of Ukraine, and recent changes in tax legislation affecting the IT industry.

As head of the Academy’s Department of Information Policy, guest speaker Prof. Svitlana Chukut outlined the forum’s history, aims and preliminary programme. She explained how e-governance could support public administration reform and described the forum as an opportunity to compare international practice and showcase initiatives from Ukraine’s national and local authorities.

She noted that deputy heads and department heads responsible for e-governance in central executive bodies and regional administrations were expected to attend. She invited interested companies and organisations to take part. The forum was expected to produce recommendations for the responsible government authorities.
